INTRODUCTION TO BOOKS III
AND IV

Herodotus' narrative in the Third Book of his history is extremely discursive and episodic. It may be briefly summarized as follows:

Chapters 1 to 38 deal mainly with Cambyses. They relate the Persian invasion and conquest of Egypt, Cambyses' failed expedition against the Ethiopians, and the sacrilegious and cruel acts of the latter part of his reign. The section 38–60 begins with an account of Polycrates of Samos and his relations with Amasis of Egypt, and continues with a narrative of Polycrates' war against his banished subjects. The fact that these latter were aided not only by Spartans but by Corinthians serves to introduce the story of the domestic feuds of Periander, despot of Corinth. Chapter 61 resumes the story of Cambyses; the Magian usurpation of the Persian throne, Cambyses' death, the counterplot against and ultimate overthrow of the pseudo-Smerdis and his brother by seven Persian conspirators, and the accession of Darius—all this is narrated with much

vii

INTRODUCTION TO BOOKS III AND IV

picturesque and dramatic detail in twenty-eight chapters (61–88). Then follows a list of Darius' tributary provinces (88–97), supplemented by various unconnected details relating to Arabia and India (98–117). The next thirty-two chapters (118–149) narrate various events in the early part of Darius' reign: the fate of Polycrates of Samos; the insolence and death of his murderer Oroetes; how Democedes, a Samian physician, rose to power at the Persian court and was sent with a Persian commission to reconnoiter Greek coasts; how Polycrates' brother Syloson regained with Persian help the sovereignty of Samos. Lastly, chapters 150–160 describe the revolt and second capture of Babylon.

Book IV begins with the intention of describing Darius' invasion of Scythia, and more than two-thirds of the book is devoted to Scythian geography and history. Chapters 1–15 deal with the legendary origin of the Scythians; 16–31 with the population of the country and the climate of the far north; this leads to a discussion of the Hyperboreans and their alleged commerce with the Aegean (32–36), and (37–45) a parenthetical section showing the relationship of Europe, Asia, and Libya to one another. The story of a circumnavigation of Libya forms part of this section. Chapters 46–58 enumerate the rivers of Scythia, and 59–82 describe its manners and customs.

Darius' passage of the Hellespont and the Danube is

viii

INTRODUCTION TO BOOKS III AND IV

narrated in chapters 83–98. Chapters 99–117 are once more parenthetic, describing first the general outline of Scythia, and next giving some details as to neighbouring tribes, with the story of the Amazons. From 118 to 144 Herodotus professes to relate the movements of the Persian and Scythian armies, till Darius returns to the Danube and thence to Asia again.

The Libyan part of the book begins at 145. Twenty-three chapters (145–167) give the history of Cyrene, its colonisation from Greece and the fortunes of its rulers till the time of Darius, when it was brought into contact with Persia by the appeal of its exiled queen Pheretime to the Persian governor of Egypt, who sent an army to recover Cyrene for her. The thirty-two following chapters (168–199) are a detailed description of Libya: 168–180, the Libyan seaboard from Egypt to the Tritonian lake; 181–190, the sandy ridge inland stretching (according to Herodotus) from Thebes in Egypt to the Atlas; 191–199, in the main, Libya west of the "Tritonian lake." At chapter 200 the story of Pheretime is resumed and the capture of Barce described. The book ends with the death of Pheretime and the disastrous return to Egypt of her Persian allies.

The above brief abstract shows that Book IV, at least, is full of geography and ethnology. It is, I believe, generally held that Herodotus himself

ix

INTRODUCTION TO BOOKS III AND IV

As a general rule, the farther from home Herodotus is, the farther he also is from reality.
   It follows from this that the more distant Herodotus' narrative of events is from the Greek world and his possible sources of information, the more it is filled, for us, with geographical difficulties. It is probable that, as he tells us, "Scythians" did at some point invade the Black Sea coasts and dispossess an earlier population of "Cimmerians," whom they perhaps pursued into Asia. The bare fact may well be true; but Herodotus' description of how it happened cannot be reconciled with geographical reality. The whole story is confused; the Cimmerians could not have fled along the coast of the Black Sea, as Herodotus states — that would apparently have been a physical impossibility. In such cases, the stricter school of critics was sometimes tempted to dismiss an entire narrative as a collection of lies. More charitably, modern scholars sometimes do their best to bring the historian's detailed account into some sort of harmony with the map, by emending the text or by other means. But if the former approach was unjust, the latter is wasted effort. There is surely only one conclusion to draw, and a very obvious one: that Herodotus was misinformed about geographical conditions. Ignorance lies at the root of the matter. Herodotus did not have the geographical knowledge needed for describing the movements of tribes on the north

INTRODUCTION TO BOOKS III AND IV

units, appear in other passages in Herodotus as subjects of a single satrapy. What the historian gives us in Book III is simply a statistical list of Darius' revenues and the sources from which they were drawn.

HERODOTUS
BOOK III

VOL. II.                                                                                               B

HERODOTUS: HISTORIES

Book III

1. It was against this Amasis that Cambyses son of Cyrus marched to war, bringing with him, among others over whom he ruled, Greeks of Ionia and Aeolia. His reason was as follows. Cambyses had sent a herald to Egypt to ask Amasis for his daughter, and he made this request on the advice of an Egyptian who bore a grudge against Amasis, because Amasis had taken him from all the physicians in Egypt and torn him away from his wife and children to hand him over to the Persians, when Cyrus had sent to Amasis requesting the best eye-doctor in Egypt. It was out of resentment over this that the Egyptian urged Cambyses to ask for the daughter of Amasis, so that Amasis would either suffer grief by giving her, or make an enemy of Cambyses by refusing. Amasis, troubled by the power of the Persians and at a loss, could neither give his daughter nor refuse; for he knew well that Cambyses intended to keep her not as a wife but as a concubine. Thinking the matter over, he did the following. There was a daughter of the former king Apries, tall and beautiful, the only one left of that house, whose name was

HERODOTUS

BOOK III

1. It was against this Amasis that Cambyses led an army of his subjects, Ionian and Aeolian Greeks among them. This was his reason: Cambyses sent a herald to Egypt asking Amasis for his daughter; and he did this on the advice of a certain Egyptian, who conceived the plan out of a grudge he held against Amasis, because when Cyrus had sent to Amasis asking for the best eye-doctor in Egypt, the king had chosen this man from among all the Egyptian physicians and sent him forcibly to Persia, separating him from his wife and children. Nursing this grudge, he persuaded Cambyses to ask Amasis for his daughter, so that Amasis would be distressed if he gave her, or would become Cambyses' enemy if he refused. Amasis was deeply afraid of the power of Persia, and could neither give his daughter nor refuse; for he knew well that Cambyses would make her not his queen but his mistress. Thinking this over, he decided upon a very tall and beautiful young woman named Nitetis, daughter of the former king Apries, and all that remained of that

¹ The accepted date is 525 B.C.

Her name was Nitetis. Amasis dressed this girl in fine clothing and gold jewelry and sent her to Persia as his own daughter. After some time, when the king greeted her by calling her by her father's name, the girl said to him: "O King, you do not realize that you have been deceived by Amasis. He adorned me and sent me as his own daughter, when in truth I am the daughter of Apries, his former master, whom Amasis murdered after rising up against him together with the Egyptians." This speech, and the grievance it planted in him, drove Cambyses, son of Cyrus, in great anger, to march against Egypt.

2. This is the account the Persians give. The Egyptians, however, claim Cambyses as one of their own, saying that he was born of this very daughter of Apries — that it was Cyrus, not Cambyses, who sent to Amasis for his daughter. But in saying this they are wrong. And it has not escaped their own notice (for if any people know Persian customs, the Egyptians do) that first, it is not their law for a bastard to reign when a legitimate heir exists, and second, that Cambyses was the son of Cassandane, daughter of Pharnaspes, a man of the Achaemenid family, and not of the Egyptian woman. Yet they distort the story, pretending to be kinsmen of the house of Cyrus.

3. So much for that. There is also another story told — one that I myself find unconvincing — that one of the Persian women came to visit the wives of Cyrus, and when she saw the tall and beautiful children standing beside Cassandane, she praised them extravagantly with great admiration. Cassandane, who was the wife of Cyrus, then said: "Yet though I am the mother of such children —"

4

HERODOTUS

— that Cyrus held her mother in dishonor, while he held the Egyptian woman, an acquired wife, in honor." They say that Nitetis was distressed to hear this, and that the elder of her sons, Cambyses, said: "Well then, mother, when I am a man, I will turn Egypt upside down and inside out." He was said to have been about ten years old when he said this, and the women were amazed by it. Keeping this in mind, they say, once he had grown to manhood and obtained the kingship, he undertook the campaign against Egypt.

4. Another such event also contributed to this expedition. Among the mercenaries of Amasis there was a man of Halicarnassian birth named Phanes, a man of sound judgment and brave in war. This Phanes, having some grievance against Amasis, escaped by ship from Egypt, wishing to have an audience with Cambyses. Since he was a man of no small account among the mercenaries and had the most precise knowledge of Egyptian affairs, Amasis made every effort to catch him, and sent after him his most trusted eunuch in a trireme. This man caught up with Phanes in Lycia, but did not bring him back to Egypt, for Phanes outwitted him: he got the guards drunk and slipped away to the Persians. When Cambyses was eager to march against Egypt but was at a loss about the march — specifically how to cross the waterless desert — Phanes came to him and told him all about Amasis's affairs, and also advised him on the route, counseling him to send to the king of the Arabs and ask him to grant safe passage through his territory.

5. For there are only these evident routes of entry into

6

Egypt. For from Phoenicia to the borders of the city of Cadytis belongs to the Syrians called Palestinians; and from Cadytis, a city which is, in my estimation, not much smaller than Sardis, the trading-posts along the coast as far as the city of Ienysus belong to the Arabian, and from Ienysus again to the Serbonian marsh, along which Mount Casius stretches down to the sea, these belong to the Syrians; and from the Serbonian marsh, in which Typhon is said by legend to be hidden, from that point Egypt begins. The region between the city of Ienysus and Mount Casius and the Serbonian marsh, which is no small stretch of land but extends about a three days' journey, is terribly lacking in water.

6. I will now describe something that few of those who sail to Egypt have noticed. Into Egypt, from all of Greece and also from Phoenicia, pottery jars full of wine are imported twice a year, and yet one might say that there is practically not a single empty wine jar to be seen anywhere. Where then, one might ask, do they all go? I will explain this as well: each local magistrate is required to collect all the jars from his own town and bring them to Memphis, and those at Memphis must fill them with water and transport them to those waterless regions of Syria. Thus the pottery that keeps arriving and being unloaded in Egypt makes its way, once emptied, back to Syria.

7. Such then were the Persians who prepared this invasion route into Egypt, and accordingly

This is the situation. The road runs from Phoenicia as far as the city of Cadytis, which belongs to the Syrians of Palestine, as the region is called. From Cadytis — which, in my estimation, is a city not much smaller than Sardis — to the city of Ienysus, the seaports belong to the Arabs. From Ienysus onward they are Syrian again, all the way to the Serbonian marsh, beside which the Casian promontory juts out into the sea. From this Serbonian marsh, where Typhon is said to have been hidden, begins Egypt. Now between Ienysus and the Casian mountain and the Serbonian marsh there lies a wide stretch of territory — as much as three days' journey — remarkably waterless.

6. I will now tell of something that very few of those who sail to Egypt have noticed. Earthen jars full of wine are brought into Egypt twice a year from all over Greece and from Phoenicia as well; yet there is not, so to speak, a single empty wine jar to be seen anywhere in the country. What, one might ask, becomes of them all? I will explain that too. Each district governor must collect all the earthen pots from his own township and bring them to Memphis, and the people of Memphis must fill them with water and carry them out to those waterless regions of Syria. So the earthen pottery that is imported into Egypt and sold there is transported to Syria to replenish the supply that originally came from there.

7. Now as soon as the Persians took possession of Egypt, it was they who took over the responsibility of supplying the entry

¹ Probably Gaza.
² Hot winds and volcanic activity were attributed by Greek mythology to Typhon, who had been cast down from heaven by Zeus and "buried" in hot or volcanic regions. Typhon came to be identified with the Egyptian god Set, and the legend grew that he was buried in the Serbonian marsh.

HERODOTUS

...having packed the aforementioned things with water, as soon as they took possession of Egypt. At that time, since water was not yet ready, Cambyses, having learned of this from his guest-friend of Halicarnassus, sent messengers to the Arabian and made his request, and obtained safe conduct, giving and receiving pledges from him.

8. The Arabians hold pledges among men in the highest regard, and they make them in the following manner: another man, standing between the two who wish to make the pledge, cuts with a sharp stone the inner part of the hands of both parties near the thumbs, and then taking a tuft of wool from the garment of each, smears with the blood seven stones lying between them; while doing this he calls upon Dionysus and Urania. When this is done, the one who has made the pledge commends the stranger, or likewise the townsman, if the pledge is made with a townsman, to his friends; and the friends consider it their duty to honor the pledge as well. They believe that Dionysus and Urania are the only gods, and they say that they cut their hair in the same way that Dionysus himself had his hair cut; they cut it in a circular fashion, shaving the temples. They call Dionysus Orotalt, and Urania Alilat.

9. When the Arabian had made his pledge to the messengers who had come from Cambyses, he devised the following plan: he filled camel-skins with water and loaded them onto all his living camels, and having done this he drove them into the waterless desert and waited there for Cambyses' army. This is the more plausible of the accounts that are told; but one must also

10

the less credible, since it is said to have been spoken. There is a great river in Arabia called the Corys, which flows out into the sea called the Red Sea. From this river the king of the Arabians is said to have sewn together hides of raw ox and other skins into a conduit long enough to reach to the waterless region, and through it to have brought the water; and in the waterless region he had great cisterns dug to receive and preserve the water. It is a twelve days' journey from the river to this waterless land. The water was brought through three conduits to three different places.

10. At the mouth of the Nile called the Pelusian mouth, Psammenitus son of Amasis was encamped, waiting for Cambyses. For Cambyses did not find Amasis alive when he marched against Egypt; Amasis had died after a reign of forty-four years, during which no great misfortune had befallen him. After his death he was embalmed and buried in the tomb which he had built for himself in the sanctuary. In the reign of Psammenitus son of Amasis over Egypt, the greatest portent ever seen by the Egyptians occurred: the Egyptian Thebes was rained upon, a thing that had never happened before or since up to my time, as the Thebans themselves say; for the upper parts of Egypt receive no rain at all; but at that time Thebes was rained upon in drops.

11. When the Persians had crossed the waterless region and encamped near the Egyptians in preparation for battle, the mercenaries of the Egyptian king, who were Greeks and Carians, in their anger

BOOK III. 9-11

This story is also hard to believe, yet they tell it nonetheless. There is a great river in Arabia called Corys, which flows into the sea called the Red Sea. From this river, the king of the Arabians is said to have transported water through a pipe made of sewn ox-hides and other hides, long enough to reach the dry desert region. He also had large cisterns dug in that region to collect and store the water. The journey from the river to that desert takes twelve days. Through three pipes, they say, he directed the water to three separate locations.

10. Psammenitus, the son of Amasis, had encamped at the mouth of the Nile known as the Pelusian mouth, waiting for Cambyses. For when Cambyses marched against Egypt, he found that Amasis was no longer alive — he had died after a reign of forty-four years, during which no great disaster had befallen him. After his death he was embalmed and laid in the tomb he had built for himself within the temple. While his son Psammenitus was king of Egypt, the people witnessed a most remarkable event: rain fell at Thebes in Egypt, where, as the Thebans themselves attest, there had never been rain before, nor has there been since within my own lifetime — for indeed there is no rain at all in the upper reaches of Egypt. Yet at that time a light drizzle fell at Thebes.¹

11. Now the Persians, having crossed the waterless desert and encamped near the Egyptians with the intention of giving battle, the foreign soldiers serving the Egyptians — Greeks and Carians — devised a plan to punish Phanes,

¹ In modern times there is occasionally a little rain at Thebes (Luxor), but very little and very rarely.

against Phanes for having led a foreign army against Egypt, they devised the following scheme against him. Phanes had left his sons behind in Egypt; these they brought to the camp and into their father's sight, and set a great bowl between the two armies. Then they brought the sons one by one and cut their throats over the bowl; and when they had gone through all the sons, they poured wine and water into the bowl, and all the mercenaries drank of the blood and so joined battle. The fighting was fierce, and great numbers fell on both sides, but in the end the Egyptians were routed.

12. I saw a great marvel, which I learned of from the local inhabitants. The bones of those who fell in this battle lay scattered separately — the Persian bones in one place, just as they had been separated from the start, and the Egyptian bones in another. The skulls of the Persians are so weak that if you strike one with a mere pebble you will pierce it through; but those of the Egyptians are so strong that you could hardly break one even with a heavy stone. The reason they gave for this, and it easily persuaded me, is that the Egyptians shave their heads from childhood, and the bone thickens through exposure to the sun. This same practice is also why so few of them go bald — you would see fewer bald men among the Egyptians than among any other people. This, then, is why their skulls are strong; and the reason the Persians have weak skulls is this: they keep their heads in the shade from the beginning, wearing felt caps called tiaras. So much for this.

now such things as these. I also saw other similar remains at Papremis of those who were destroyed along with Achaemenes son of Darius by Inaros the Libyan.

13. When the Egyptians were routed in the battle, they fled in complete disorder. Cambyses, with them shut up in Memphis, sent up the river a Mytilenean vessel carrying a Persian herald to invite the Egyptians to terms of surrender. But when they saw the vessel sailing into Memphis, they poured out from the walls en masse, destroyed the ship, and tore the men limb from limb, carrying the pieces back inside the walls. After this the Egyptians held out for a time under siege, but eventually yielded. The neighboring Libyans, frightened by what had happened in Egypt, surrendered without a fight, imposed tribute upon themselves, and sent gifts. The Cyrenaeans and Barcaeans, equally frightened as the Libyans, did likewise. Cambyses received the gifts that came from the Libyans with goodwill, but he was displeased with those that came from the Cyrenaeans — in my opinion because the amount was too small, for the Cyrenaeans had sent only five hundred silver minas. He took these up with his own hands and scattered them among his troops.

14. On the tenth day after Cambyses had taken the fortress at Memphis, he placed Psammenitus, king of the Egyptians — who had reigned only six months — in the city's outskirts together with other Egyptians, intending to humiliate him, and proceeded to test his spirit in the following manner. He dressed Psammenitus's daughter in the garb of a slave and sent her out to fetch water carrying a water-jar, and along with her he sent other maidens chosen from the daughters of the leading men, dressed likewise,

BOOK III. 12-14

also the skulls of those Persians who fell at Papremis fighting alongside Achaemenes, son of Darius, against the Libyan Inaros — and these were in the same condition as the others.

13. After their defeat in battle, the Egyptians fled in disorder; driven back to Memphis, they found themselves faced with Cambyses, who sent a Persian herald upriver in a Mytilenean ship to propose terms of agreement. But when the Egyptians saw the ship approaching Memphis, they poured out en masse from their walls, destroyed the vessel, tore the crew apart — literally butchering them — and dragged the bodies back inside the walls. After that the Egyptians were put under siege and eventually surrendered. Meanwhile, the neighboring Libyans, terrified by what had happened in Egypt, gave themselves up without a fight, imposing tribute on themselves and sending gifts. The people of Cyrene and Barca, equally frightened, did the same. Cambyses accepted the gifts of the Libyans graciously, but when the offerings from Cyrene arrived, he snatched them up and scattered them with his own hands among his troops. I believe he did this to show his contempt for the smallness of the gift, since the Cyrenaeans had sent only five hundred silver minas.

14. Ten days after the walled city of Memphis surrendered, Cambyses took Psammenitus, king of Egypt — who had reigned for only six months — and seated him in the outskirts of the city along with other Egyptians, intending to humiliate him. Having done so, he then set out to test Psammenitus' character, as I shall describe. He dressed the king's daughter in the clothes of a slave and sent her out with a jug to fetch water, accompanied by other girls of noble birth dressed the same way, chosen from

...dressed in the manner of the king's command. As the maidens passed by their fathers with weeping and lamentation, all the others cried out and wept in return at seeing their children so ill-treated, but Psammenitus, when he saw and understood what was happening, bowed his head to the ground. After the water-carriers had passed, next came his son, led along with two thousand other Egyptians of the same age, their necks bound with rope and their mouths bridled; they were being led to pay the penalty for the Mytilenaeans who had perished with their ship at Memphis. For the royal judges had decreed that for each man ten of the foremost Egyptians should die in return. When he saw them passing by and understood that his son was being led to his death, while the other Egyptians sitting around him wept and made loud lamentation, Psammenitus did the same as he had done at the sight of his daughter. After these too had passed, it happened that one of his former drinking companions — an older man who had been stripped of all his possessions and had nothing beyond what a beggar has, and who was begging from the army — passed by Psammenitus and the Egyptians sitting in the suburb. When Psammenitus saw him, he burst into loud weeping, called his companion by name, and beat himself on the head. Guards were posted near him, who reported to Cambyses everything he did at each procession. Cambyses, marveling at what was happening, sent a messenger to question him, saying the following: "Your master Cambyses asks you, Psammenitus, why it is that seeing your daughter dishonored and your son being led to his death you neither cried out nor lamented, yet—"

...you wept, yet you honored the beggar who is nothing to you, as though inquiring about others." So he asked these questions, and the other replied as follows: "O son of Cyrus, my own personal sufferings were too great for weeping, but the grief for my companion deserved tears — a man who, having fallen from great prosperity and good fortune into beggary, has arrived at the threshold of old age." And when these words were reported back by Psammenitus, they seemed to the Persians to have been well spoken; and, as the Egyptians tell it, Croesus wept (for he too had come along following Cambyses to Egypt), and the Persians present wept, and even Cambyses himself was touched by some pity, and he immediately ordered that Psammenitus's son be saved from those being put to death, and that Psammenitus himself be brought up from the suburb and conducted into his presence.

15. Those who went to fetch the son found him no longer alive, but already cut down first; but they raised up Psammenitus and brought him before Cambyses. There he lived out his remaining days suffering no violence. And had he been trusted not to meddle, he would have received Egypt back to govern as its administrator, since the Persians are accustomed to honor the sons of kings; even when kings have rebelled against them, they nevertheless give the kingship back to their children. There are many other examples by which one may judge that this is their established custom — notably in the case of Thannyras son of Inaros, who received back the authority his father had held, and in that of Pausiris son of Amyrtaeus; for he too received back his father's authority. Yet no people had ever done the Persians more and greater harm than Inaros and Amyrtaeus...

they had accomplished. Now Psammenitus, plotting harm, received his just reward: for he was caught trying to incite the Egyptians to revolt. When this was discovered by Cambyses, he drank bull's blood and died on the spot. That was how he met his end.

16. Cambyses traveled from Memphis to the city of Sais, intending to do exactly what he then did. When he entered the palace of Amasis, he immediately ordered the corpse of Amasis to be brought out from its tomb. Once this was done, he commanded his men to flog it, pull out its hair, prick it, and inflict every other kind of outrage upon it. When they grew weary of this — for the corpse, being embalmed, held together and did not fall apart — Cambyses ordered it to be burned, an impious command; for the Persians consider fire to be a god. To burn the dead is therefore contrary to the custom of either people: for the Persians, for the reason already stated, since they hold it wrong to give the corpse of a human being to a god; while among the Egyptians, fire is considered a living beast that devours everything it seizes, and when gorged with its food, dies together with what it has consumed. It is therefore not at all their custom to give a corpse to wild beasts, which is why they embalm their dead — so that the body may not lie and be eaten by worms. Thus Cambyses was ordering what was contrary to the custom of both peoples. However, as the Egyptians say, it was not Amasis who suffered these indignities, but another Egyptian of the same age as Amasis, upon whom the Persians vented their abuse, thinking they were abusing Amasis. For they say that Amasis had learned from an oracle what was to happen to his body after death,

BOOK III. 15-16

and Amyrtaeus. But as things turned out, Psammenitus plotted treachery and got what he deserved; he was caught trying to stir up a revolt among the Egyptians, and when word of this reached Cambyses, Psammenitus drank bulls' blood and died immediately. That was how his life ended.

16. From Memphis Cambyses traveled to the city of Sais, intending to do exactly what he then did. He entered the house of Amasis and immediately ordered that Amasis' body be taken from its tomb. When this was done, he commanded his men to flog the corpse, tear out its hair, and abuse it in every other way possible. When they grew tired of this — for the body, having been embalmed, held together and did not fall apart — Cambyses ordered it to be burned. This was a sacrilegious act, since the Persians regard fire as a god. Neither nation, therefore, considers it right to burn the dead: the Persians, for the reason just stated, say it is wrong to give a human corpse to a god; while the Egyptians believe fire is a living creature that devours whatever it catches and, when it has eaten its fill, dies along with what it has consumed. Since it is absolutely not their custom to feed the dead to animals, they embalm corpses so that they will not lie and be eaten by worms. So Cambyses ordered something that went against the customs of both peoples. The Egyptians say, however, that it was not actually Amasis whose body suffered this treatment, but another Egyptian of similar age, whom the Persians abused in the belief that they were treating Amasis this way. Their account holds that Amasis had learned from an oracle what was destined to happen,

1 The revolt of the Egyptians Inaros and Amyrtaeus against the Persian governor lasted from 460 to 455 B.C.
2 The blood was supposed to coagulate and choke the drinker. (How and Wells, ad loc.)

23

HERODOTUS

...about to happen, and having heard these things, he buried this man who had been flogged and had died at the entrance doors, within his own tomb, and commanded his son to place himself as deep in the inner recess of the tomb as possible. Now these instructions of Amasis concerning the burial and this man do not seem to me to have had any real basis, but the Egyptians make a solemn matter of them.

17. After these events, Cambyses planned three military campaigns: one against the Carthaginians, one against the Ammonians, and one against the long-lived Ethiopians, who dwell on the southern sea of Libya. In his deliberation he decided to send the naval force against the Carthaginians, to detach a part of his infantry against the Ammonians, and to send spies first to the Ethiopians, to observe whether what is called the Table of the Sun actually exists among these Ethiopians, and to survey everything else there as well, ostensibly bringing gifts to their king.

18. The royal judges are men chosen from among the Persians to serve until they die or are found to have acted unjustly; through them the Persians conduct their legal proceedings, and they serve as interpreters of ancestral ordinances, and everything is referred to them. When Cambyses questioned them, they gave him an answer that was both just and safe: they said they could find no law commanding a brother to live with his sister, but they had found another law, that the king of the Persians might do whatever he wished. Cambyses was delighted watching this, but the woman sitting beside him wept. they are thinking rightly. they carry around on the prows of the triremes. For anyone who has not seen these, I will explain: they are likenesses of a pygmy man. 38. It is clear to me from every angle that Cambyses was greatly mad; for otherwise he would not have set about mocking sacred rites and customs. For if one were to propose to all people that they choose the finest customs from all the customs that exist, each group, after due consideration, would choose their own; so strongly does each people believe that their own customs are by far the finest. It is therefore not likely that anyone but a madman would make a mockery of such things. That all people hold this view about their customs can be established by many other pieces of evidence, and in particular by this one. Darius, during his reign, summoned the Greeks who were present at his court and asked them for what sum of money they would be willing to eat the bodies of their fathers when they died; they answered that they would not do this for any amount. After this, Darius summoned those Indians called Callatians, who do eat their parents, and asked them in the presence of the Greeks, who learned what was being said through an interpreter, for what payment they would be willing to burn their dead fathers with fire; they cried out loudly and told him to keep silent. Such are the established customs, and it seems to me that Pindar was right when he said in his poem that custom is king of all.

He did this so that when some terrible and great disaster overtook Polycrates, he himself would not feel grief in his heart as he would for a guest-friend.

Some say that those Samians sent away by Polycrates never reached Egypt, but that when they were sailing and found themselves off Carpathus, they took counsel among themselves and decided to sail no further. There are those who say that the men returning from Egypt defeated Polycrates, but in my opinion they are wrong; for if they had been capable of subduing Polycrates on their own, there would have been no need to call upon the Lacedaemonians. Polycrates had rounded up the wives and children of the citizens under his control and confined them in the shipsheds, ready to burn them along with the sheds if those citizens should betray him to the returning men.

52. Finally Periander issued a proclamation that whoever received him into their home or spoke with him would owe a sacred fine to Apollo, the amount of which he specified. In view of this proclamation, no one was willing either to speak with him or to receive him into their house; and moreover, the boy himself did not think it right to attempt what had been forbidden, but persisted in wandering about in the colonnades. On the fourth day, Periander saw him brought low by lack of washing and lack of food, and felt pity for him. Relenting from his anger, he approached and said: "My son, which of these two is preferable — the life you are now living, or to inherit the tyranny and all the good things I now possess, as is fitting for a son to receive from his father? You, who are my son and the king of prosperous Corinth, have chosen a vagrant's life, setting yourself in opposition and in anger toward one against whom you had least reason to do so. For if some misfortune has occurred, from which you harbor suspicion against me, that misfortune has fallen upon me too, and I am the greater sharer in it, to the extent that I myself brought it about. But now that you have learned how much better it is to be envied than to be pitied, and what it means to be angry at one's parents and at one's betters, go back home." With these words Periander tried to win him over; but the boy gave no other answer to his father than to say that Periander owed a sacred fine to the god for coming to speak with him. Then Periander, realizing that the trouble with his son was intractable and beyond overcoming, sent him out of his sight, dispatching him by ship to Corcyra — for he ruled over that island too.

Having dispatched him, Periander made war on his father-in-law Procles, regarding him as the chief cause of his present troubles, and he captured Epidaurus and took Procles himself prisoner.

Many people prefer what is reasonable over strict justice, and many already, in seeking their mother's inheritance, have thrown away their father's. Tyranny is a precarious thing, and it has many lovers — and your father is old now and past his prime. Do not give away what is yours to others." She said all the most persuasive things she had been coached to say by her father. But he answered that he would never come to Corinth as long as he knew his father was still alive. 54. When the Lacedaemonians arrived with a great fleet, they besieged Samos. I myself met at Pitane a man of the third generation descended from this Archias — another Archias, son of Samios son of Archias — who honored the Samians more than any other foreigners, and said that his father had been given the name Samios because his own father Archias had died gloriously in Samos. He said he honored the Samians because they had given his grandfather a public funeral.

60. I have spoken at greater length about the Samians because they have three works that are the greatest of all works among the Greeks: first, a tunnel driven from below through a mountain eight hundred and fifty feet high, with an opening at each end. The length of the tunnel is seven stades, and the height and width are each eight feet. Throughout its entire length another channel has been dug, twenty cubits deep and three feet wide, through which the water is carried by pipes and so brought to the city from a great spring. The architect of this tunnel was Eupalinus of Megara, son of Naustrophus. This is one of the three works; the second is a mole in the sea around the harbor, twenty fathoms deep, and more than two stades in length. The third is the temple, which is the largest of all temples we know; its first architect was Rhoecus son of Phileus, a native of the island. It is for these reasons that I have dwelt longer on the affairs of Samos.

They therefore believed that Smerdis son of Cyrus was the reigning king; for Prexaspes also vehemently denied that he had killed Smerdis, since after Cambyses was dead it was not safe for him to say that he had killed the son of Cyrus with his own hand.

80. When the tumult had died down and more than five days had passed, those who had revolted against the Magi deliberated about the state of all affairs, and speeches were made which some Greeks find incredible, yet they were indeed made. Otanes urged that power be placed in the hands of the Persian people, speaking as follows: "It seems to me that one man among us should no longer be monarch. For it is neither pleasant nor good. You have seen to what lengths the arrogance of Cambyses went, and you have had your share of the Magian's arrogance too. How can monarchy be a well-ordered thing, when it allows the ruler to do whatever he wishes with no accountability? Even the best of all men, placed in this position, would be moved outside his accustomed ways of thinking. For arrogance grows in him from the good things he possesses, and envy is inborn in man from the beginning. Possessing these two things, he has every sort of wickedness: for swollen with arrogance he does many reckless deeds, and others he does out of envy. And yet a tyrant ought to be free of envy, seeing that he has all good things. But his nature toward his citizens is the very opposite: he envies the best men who survive and live, takes pleasure in the worst of the citizens, and is most ready to receive slanders against them. Most inconsistent of all: if you admire him moderately, he is offended that he is not being lavishly attended upon, and if you do attend upon him

If someone finds out, he is deeply resentful, as one would be toward a flatterer. But now I come to the most important points: he overturns ancestral customs, he violates women, and he puts men to death without trial. Rule by the many, on the other hand, has first of all the finest of all names: equality under the law. Second, it does none of the things that a monarch does. Offices are assigned by lot, those who hold office are accountable for their conduct, and all decisions are referred to the common assembly. I therefore propose that we abandon monarchy and raise up the power of the people, for in the many lies everything."

Megabyzus next urged that they entrust power to an oligarchy, speaking as follows: "What Otanes said about ending tyranny, let that stand as my view as well; but in urging that power be given to the people, he has missed the best course. At least when a tyrant acts, he acts with knowledge; but the people do not even have that capacity — for how could they have knowledge, when they have never been taught anything good nor seen any good thing of their own? They rush into affairs without understanding, like a winter torrent. Let those who wish harm to the Persians make use of the people; but let us choose a body of the best men and invest them with power — for we ourselves shall be among them — and it is natural that the best men produce the best decisions."

Third, Darius put forward his opinion, saying: "To me, what Megabyzus said concerning the multitude seems rightly spoken, but what he said concerning oligarchy does not. For of the three options set before us, each said to be the best in argument — the best democracy, oligarchy, and monarchy — I say that monarchy is far superior. For nothing could prove better than the rule of a single best man; using such judgment, he would govern the people blamelessly, and plans against hostile men would be kept secret most effectively under this system. In an oligarchy, when many men are practicing virtue for the common good, fierce personal enmities tend to arise; for each man, wishing to be the foremost and to have his own opinion prevail, they come into great hostility with one another, from which factions arise, and from factions come killings; and from killings the outcome is monarchy — and in this it is shown by how much monarchy is the best. Such a person is then admired by the people, and being admired, he is revealed as a monarch — and in this he too demonstrates that monarchy is the best. 98. The Indians obtain the great quantity of gold, from which they bring the gold dust mentioned to the king, in the following manner. To the east of the Indian territory there is sand; for of all the peoples of Asia that we know of, and about whom something reliable is reported, the Indians are the first toward the dawn and the rising sun; east of the Indians is desert because of the sand. There are many Indian peoples, not all speaking the same language, and some of them are nomads and some are not; some live in the river marshes and eat raw fish, which they catch from reed boats — each boat made from a single joint of reed. These particular Indians wear garments of bark: when they cut and beat bark from the river, they weave it like a mat and wear it like a breastplate.

99. Other Indians, living to the east of these, are nomads who eat raw flesh; they are called Padaeans, and they are said to follow customs such as these: whenever one of their community falls ill, whether woman or man, the man's closest companions kill him, saying that his flesh would be ruined for them if he wasted away with sickness; though he denies that he is ill, they do not accept it, but kill him and feast upon him. If a woman falls ill, the women who are her closest companions do the same as the men do to theirs. And indeed, one who reaches old age they sacrifice and feast upon; but few reach this point, for

many of them survive; for they kill everyone who falls sick before the sickness takes hold.

100. There is yet another different custom among certain Indians: they kill no living creature, nor do they sow anything, nor is it their custom to own houses; they eat grass. There is a grain the size of millet, which grows of itself from the earth within a husk; this they gather and boil in the husk itself and eat it. Whoever among them falls sick goes to the desert and lies down there; no one gives any thought to him, whether he is dying or ill.

101. The sexual intercourse of all these Indians I have described is open, like that of cattle, and they all have a similar complexion, much like the Ethiopians. The semen which they discharge into their women is not white as in other men, but black like their skin; and the Ethiopians likewise discharge such seed. These Indians live farther from the Persians than any others and toward the south wind, and they were never subjects of Darius.

102. Other Indians live near the city of Caspatyrus and the land of Pactyice, dwelling to the north and north wind of the rest of the Indians, and their way of life resembles that of the Bactrians. These are the most warlike of the Indians, and it is they who are sent out to get the gold; for in that region there is a desert on account of the sand. In this desert and sandy region there are ants that are smaller than dogs but larger than foxes; some of them are kept at the palace of the Persian king, having been caught there. These ants

...of which the ants, making their homes underground, bring up the sand, just as the ants in Greece do in the same manner; and they are themselves very similar in appearance; and the sand that is brought up contains gold. 103. As for the appearance of the camel, I will not describe it to those Greeks who are already familiar with it; but what they do not know about it, I will tell: the camel has in its hind legs four thigh-bones and four knee-joints, and its genitals are turned toward the tail between the hind legs.

104. The Indians then, using such a method and such a team, drive out to collect the gold, timing their arrival to be there during the greatest heat of the day; for under the heat the ants disappear underground. Now among these people the sun is hottest in the morning, not as among others at midday, but from its rising until the hour when the market disperses. During this time it burns far more fiercely than it does at midday in Greece, so much so that they are said at that time to cool themselves in water. At midday the sun burns them much the same as it does other peoples. As afternoon comes on, the sun becomes for them like the morning sun

just as the morning sun warms all others, and as it moves away from that point it grows colder still, until by the time it is in the west it is at its coldest.

105. When the Indians arrive at the place carrying their sacks, they fill them with the sand as quickly as possible and drive back at full speed; for the ants, according to what the Persians say, smell them out at once and give chase. They say that nothing is equal to these ants in speed, so that if the Indians did not get a head start while the ants were still gathering, not one of them would escape. The male camels, being slower runners than the females, tire and are left behind, one at a time, not both together; but the females, remembering the young they have left behind, show no slackening. In this way, according to the Persians, the Indians get the greater part of their gold; there is also some that is dug from the earth, but this is less plentiful.

106. It seems that the lands at the edges of the inhabited world were allotted the finest things, just as Greece was allotted by far the finest seasons. India lies furthest to the east of all inhabited lands, as I said a little while ago; and in India all living creatures, four-footed and winged alike, are much larger than those elsewhere, except for the horses (which are surpassed by the Median horses, called Nesaean horses). There too gold is found in vast quantities, some dug from the earth, some washed down by rivers, and some seized in the manner I described. The wild trees there bear a fruit of wool that surpasses in beauty and quality the wool of sheep;

and Indians use clothing made from these trees.

107. To the south, Arabia is the most remote of inhabited lands, and it is the only country in the whole world where frankincense grows, along with myrrh, cassia, cinnamon, and ledanum. All of these except myrrh are obtained with great difficulty by the Arabians. They gather frankincense by burning storax, which the Phoenicians export to Greece; they obtain it by burning this resin, for the frankincense-bearing trees are guarded by small winged serpents, varied in appearance, which swarm in great numbers around each tree — the same kind that make incursions into Egypt — and nothing drives them away from the trees except the smoke of burning storax.

108. The Arabians also tell the following story: the whole earth would have been filled with these serpents, were it not for something that I have heard happens with vipers as well. And somehow the providence of God, as is fitting since it is wise, has made all creatures that are timid of spirit and good to eat very prolific, so that they do not disappear through being eaten, while those that are savage and harmful produce few offspring. The hare, for example, is hunted by every beast, bird, and human being, and so is extremely prolific; it is the only animal of all that conceives a second litter while already pregnant, and it carries young in the womb at one time that are furred, others that are bare, others that are just being formed in the womb, and yet others being conceived. 107. Arabia, moreover, is the most southerly of all inhabited lands, and it is the only country that produces frankincense, myrrh, cassia, cinnamon, and gum-mastic. All of these except myrrh are hard for the Arabians to obtain. They gather frankincense by burning storax — the resin that Phoenicians export to Greece — using its smoke to drive away the winged snakes that guard the spice-bearing trees. These small, brightly colored snakes, many coiled around each tree, are the same kind that raid Egypt. Nothing but the smoke of storax will drive them away from the trees.

108. The Arabians also say that their whole country would be overrun by these snakes were it not for the same check that I am told keeps vipers in balance. It seems that divine Providence, wisely enough, has made every creature that is timid and good to eat highly prolific, so that it will not be wiped out by predation, while creatures that are fierce and harmful produce only few offspring. The hare, for instance, is hunted by every beast, bird, and human being, and so breeds extremely fast; it is the only creature that conceives a new litter while already pregnant — some young in the womb are fully furred, some still hairless, some barely formed — even as others have already been born and are being hunted down. Such is the case. Now the lioness, being the strongest and most bold of beasts, gives birth only once in her lifetime, and gives birth to a single cub; for in the act of giving birth she expels her womb along with the cub. The reason for this is as follows: when the cub begins to stir inside the mother, it scratches the womb with its claws, which are sharper than those of any other animal, and as it grows it tears further and further with its scratchings; and when the time of birth is near, there is no part of the womb left intact.

109. In the same way, if the vipers and the winged serpents of Arabia were to reproduce as their nature would allow, human life would be impossible; but as it is, when they mate in pairs, at the very moment the male ejaculates his seed, the female seizes him by the neck and does not let go until she has gnawed through it. The male dies in this manner, but the female pays the following penalty for him: the young, while still in the womb, avenge their father by eating through their mother, gnawing through her belly to make their way out. Other snakes, which are not harmful to humans, lay eggs and hatch a great many young. Vipers are found all over the world, but the winged serpents are found only in Arabia, concentrated together there and nowhere else; and this is why they seem so numerous.

110. The Arabians obtain frankincense in this manner, and cassia in the following way. They bind up their whole body and face in hides and other skins, leaving only their eyes uncovered, and then go after the cassia, which grows in a shallow lake, around and in which...

winged creatures lodge there, most resembling bats, that screech terribly and are strong in defense; one must protect one's eyes from them while harvesting the cassia.

111. The collection of cinnamon is even more remarkable than this. Where it grows and what land nurtures it, they cannot say, except that some people, using a plausible account, claim it grows in the regions where Dionysus was raised. They say that large birds carry these sticks — what we call cinnamon, having learned the name from the Phoenicians — and carry them to nests built of mud on sheer cliff faces where no man can climb. The Arabs' device against this is as follows: they cut up the limbs of dead oxen, donkeys, and other pack animals into the largest pieces possible and bring them to these places, and having laid them near the nests they withdraw far off. The birds then fly down and carry the limbs of the pack animals up to their nests, which, being unable to bear the weight, break and fall to the ground, whereupon the men come and collect the cinnamon. That is how cinnamon is gathered and reaches other countries.

112. Ladanum, which the Arabs call ladanon, comes about in an even more wondrous way: though it is found in the most foul-smelling of places, it is the sweetest of scents. It is found clinging to the beards of he-goats, like resin from the thicket. It is useful in many perfumes, and the Arabs burn it as incense above all else.

111. As for cinnamon, they gather it in an even stranger way. Where it grows and what kind of land produces it they cannot say, except that it is reported, plausibly enough, to grow in the places where Dionysus was raised. There are, it is said, great birds that take these sticks — which the Phoenicians have taught us to call cinnamon — and carry them off to nests built of mud on mountain crags that no man can reach. The Arabian method for getting around the birds is to cut very large pieces from dead oxen, donkeys, and other beasts of burden, then place these near the eyries and withdraw to a distance. The birds then fly down (so the story goes) and carry the chunks of meat up to their nests, which, unable to bear the weight, break apart and fall down the mountainside. The Arabians then come and collect what they were after. That, it is said, is how cinnamon is gathered and makes its way from Arabia to other lands.

112. But gum-mastic, which the Greeks call ledanon and the Arabians ladanon, is produced in a yet more remarkable way. Its scent is most sweet, yet nothing smells fouler than what produces it; for it is found in the beards of he-goats, clinging to them like tree-gum. It is used in the making of many perfumes, and there is nothing the Arabians burn more often for its fragrance.

113. So much concerning spices. The land of Arabia breathes a wonderfully sweet fragrance. Arabia also has two remarkable breeds of sheep found nowhere else. One breed has tails no less than three cubits long; if these were allowed to drag on the ground, the sheep would develop sores from the tails rubbing against the earth. As it is, every shepherd there knows enough carpentry to make small carts, which they fasten under the tails, binding each animal's tail to its own little cart. The other breed of sheep has broad flat tails, up to a cubit in width.

114. Toward the south, stretching in the direction of the setting sun, Ethiopia is the last inhabited land. It produces much gold, great numbers of elephants, all manner of wild trees, ebony, and men who are the tallest, most handsome, and longest-lived of all people.

115. These, then, are the most distant lands of Asia and Libya. As for the westernmost regions of Europe, I cannot speak with certainty. I do not accept that there is a river called by barbarians the Eridanus, which empties into the northern sea, from which amber is said to come; nor do I know of any Tin Islands from which our tin is brought. The very name Eridanus betrays itself as Greek, not barbarian, being the invention of some poet. And though I have tried diligently, I have not been able to learn from any eyewitness that there is a sea on the far side of Europe.

113. I have said enough about the spices of Arabia; wonderfully sweet breezes blow from that land. The Arabians also have two remarkable kinds of sheep found nowhere else. One of these has tails no less than three cubits long. If the sheep were to drag these behind them, the tails would be injured by rubbing on the ground; but as it is, every shepherd there knows enough carpentry to make small carts, which they attach under the tails, fastening each individual sheep's tail to its own cart. The other kind of sheep has tails a full cubit wide.

114. Where the south turns toward the west, the part of the world stretching farthest toward the sunset is Ethiopia; there gold is found in great abundance, along with elephants, all manner of forest trees, and ebony; and the people there are the tallest, most handsome, and longest-lived of all human beings.

115. These, then, are the most remote parts of the world in Asia and Libya. As for the farthest western regions of Europe, I cannot speak with certainty; for I do not believe that a river the barbarians call Eridanus flows into the northern sea, from which our amber is said to come, nor do I have any knowledge of Tin-islands, from which our tin is supposed to be brought. The very name "Eridanus" gives itself away as not a foreign name but a Greek one, invented by some poet; and despite all my efforts I have not been able to find anyone who has seen with his own eyes that there is a sea beyond Europe. What we do know is this only—

HERODOTUS

...of Europe. It is from the most distant parts, then, that tin and amber come to us.

116. To the north of Europe there appears to be by far the most gold. How it is produced I cannot say with certainty either; it is said that one-eyed men called Arimaspi steal it from griffins. But I do not believe this either — that there exist one-eyed men who have all the rest of their nature like other men. In any case, the outermost regions, enclosing all other lands and shutting them in, seem to possess those things which we consider the finest and rarest.

117. There is a plain in Asia enclosed on all sides by mountains, with five passes cut through the mountains. This plain once belonged to the Chorasmians, lying on the borders of the Chorasmians themselves, the Hyrcanians, the Parthians, the Sarangians, and the Thamanaeans; but since the Persians have held power, it belongs to the king. From these encircling mountains flows a great river called the Aces. Formerly this river, divided into five channels, irrigated the lands of the peoples mentioned, each channel leading to one people. But since they have come under Persian rule, this is what has happened: the king built dams stopping up the mountain passes, and with the water's outlet blocked, the plain within the mountains becomes a great sea, since the river flows in but has no outlet anywhere. Those who previously were accustomed to use

to use the water, and not having it to use is a great calamity for them. For in winter the god sends them rain just as he does for other peoples, but in summer when they sow millet and sesame they depend on the water. When no water is allotted to them, they come to the Persians, both men and their wives, and standing at the gates of the king's palace they cry out and wail; and the king orders the gates leading to this place to be opened for those most in need. When the land has drunk its fill of the water, those gates are shut, and he orders other gates to be opened for those among the rest who are most in need. As I have heard, beyond the regular tribute he exacts large sums of money before he opens the gates.

118. So that is how things stand there. Of the seven men who had risen up against the Magus, one of them, Intaphrenes, met his end for the following act of insolence, shortly after the uprising. He wished to enter the palace and transact business with the king; for it was indeed the established custom that those who had risen against the Magus had the right of access to the king without an announcer, unless the king happened to be in bed with a woman. So Intaphrenes did not think it right that anyone should announce him, since he was one of the seven, and he wished to go straight in. But the doorkeeper and the king's messenger would not allow it, saying the king was at that moment with a woman. Intaphrenes, thinking they were lying, drew his scimitar and cut off their ears and noses, and stringing these around their necks on the horse's bridle, he bound it around their necks and sent them away.

119. They presented themselves before the king and explained the reason for what they had suffered. Darius, fearing that the six might have acted together by common agreement, summoned each one separately and tested his opinion, to see whether they approved of what had been done. When he learned that Intaphrenes had acted without their involvement, he arrested Intaphrenes himself, along with his sons and all his household, strongly suspecting that he and his kinsmen were plotting rebellion against him; he arrested them and put them in bonds to await death. The wife of Intaphrenes kept coming to the palace gates, weeping and lamenting, until by her constant repetition of this she moved Darius to pity. So he sent a messenger to tell her: "Woman, King Darius grants you the release of one of your imprisoned kinsmen, whichever one you choose." She considered and then gave her answer: "If the king grants me the life of one person, I choose my brother above all others." When Darius heard this and marveled at her reasoning, he sent word saying: "Woman, the king asks you what your thinking was, that you abandoned your husband and your children and chose instead to save your brother, who is more remote to you than your children and less dear to you than your husband." She replied: "O king, I might have another husband if a god wills it, and other children if I were to lose these; but since my father and mother are no longer living, there is no way I could have another brother. That was the reasoning behind what I said." Darius judged that the woman had spoken well, and he released the one she had asked for, and also one of her sons

the eldest, being pleased with her, he killed all the others. Of the seven, he had destroyed them immediately in the manner described.

120. It was around the time of Cambyses' illness that the following events took place. Oroites was a Persian man who had been appointed by Cyrus as governor of Sardis. He conceived a desire for an unholy deed — for without having suffered any harm from Polycrates of Samos, without having heard any idle word from him, and without even having seen him before, he desired to seize and destroy him. As most people say, the reason was as follows. 120. What I will now relate happened around the time of Cambyses' illness. The viceroy of Sardis appointed by Cyrus was Oroetes, a Persian. This man intended to do a great wrong; for although he had received no injury by deed or word from Polycrates of Samos, and had not even seen him, he conceived the desire of seizing and killing him. The reason most commonly given was this: Oroetes and another Persian named Mitrobates, governor of the province at Dascyleium, were sitting by the king's door when their conversation turned to argument and a comparison of their respective achievements. Mitrobates taunted Oroetes, saying, "You cannot be counted a real man; the island of Samos lies right next to your province, yet you have not added it to the king's dominion — an island so easy to conquer that one of its own natives rose up against its rulers with just fifteen armed men and is now its lord." Some say that Oroetes, stung by this taunt, was less concerned with punishing the man who had uttered it than with doing away by any means possible with the cause of the reproach — namely, Polycrates.

Not one of the tyrants who arose among the Syracusans is worthy of being compared in magnificence with Polycrates. Oroites killed him in a manner unworthy of telling, and then crucified him. 126. So the great good fortune of Polycrates came to the end that Amasis, king of Egypt, had foretold for him. Not long afterwards, retribution for Polycrates overtook Oroites as well. After the death of Cambyses and the reign of the Magi, Oroites remained in Sardis and rendered no service to the Persians while the Medes were wresting the empire from them. In this period of confusion he killed Mitrobates, the governor from Dascyleion, who had taunted him about the matter of Polycrates, and also Mitrobates' son Cranaspes — both men of distinction among the Persians — and committed many other acts of violence. Among these, he had a messenger sent to him by Darius killed on his return journey, because the message Oroites received was not to his liking; he set men to ambush him along the road, killed him, and made both the man and his horse disappear.

Leaving aside only the rulers of Syracuse, no Greek despot can be compared to Polycrates for magnificence. After killing him by a method not worth describing, Oroetes crucified him. As for the Samians who had been in Polycrates' retinue, Oroetes released them, telling them to be grateful to him for their freedom. Those who were not Samians, or who were servants of Polycrates' followers, he kept as slaves. So Polycrates was hung up on high, and in this way his daughter's dream came true: he was washed by Zeus when it rained, and the moisture from his body served as his anointing by the sun.

126. This was the end of Polycrates' long run of successes, just as Amasis king of Egypt had warned him it would be. Not long afterward, however, Oroetes himself was overtaken by the forces that avenged Polycrates. After Cambyses died and the Magians seized power, Oroetes remained in Sardis and did nothing to help the Persians recover the power that the Medes had taken from them. On the contrary, taking advantage of the disorder, he murdered two prominent Persians: Mitrobates, the governor of Dascyleium, who had taunted him about Polycrates, and Mitrobates' son Cranaspes. Among his many other violent acts, when a messenger arrived from Darius with a message that displeased him, he laid an ambush along the road and killed that messenger on his way home, then disposed of both the man's body and his horse.

He did not think it appropriate to send an army against him directly, since affairs were still unsettled, and he was newly come to power, while he had learned that Oroites possessed great strength — he was guarded by a thousand Persian spearmen and held the provinces of Phrygia, Lydia, and Ionia. With this in mind, Darius devised the following plan. He summoned the most distinguished of the Persians and said to them: "Persians, which of you will undertake this task for me, to accomplish it by cleverness and not by force and numbers? Where cleverness is needed, there is no work for force. Which of you, then, will either bring Oroites to me alive or kill him? He has never done the Persians any good, and has done great harm: he has destroyed two of our people, Mitrobates and his son, and he kills those who are sent to summon him on my behalf, showing intolerable insolence. 142. Samos was under the rule of Maeandrius son of Maeandrius, who had received the governorship from Polycrates. Though he wished to prove himself the most just of men, he was unable to do so. For when the news of Polycrates' death was brought to him, he did the following: first he set up an altar to Zeus the Liberator and marked off a sacred precinct around it — the very one that now stands in the suburb of the city. After he had done this, he called an assembly of all the citizens and spoke as follows: "To me, as you yourselves know, the scepter and all the power of Polycrates has been entrusted, and it is now open to me to rule over you. But I will not myself do the things for which I reproach my neighbor; for Polycrates never pleased me by lording it over men who were his equals, nor does anyone else who does such things. Polycrates has fulfilled his appointed destiny; and I now lay down the rule and proclaim equality before the law for you. However, I claim these privileges for myself as my due: from the wealth of Polycrates, six talents are to be set aside for me as a special portion, and beyond this I claim the priesthood of Zeus the Liberator for myself and for my descendants forever — I who built his temple and who now bestow freedom upon you." Such was the announcement he made to the Samians. But one of them stood up and said: "You are not even worthy to rule us, being of low birth and a scoundrel. 150. While the naval expedition was away to Samos, the Babylonians revolted, having prepared themselves very well. For during all the time that the Magus ruled and the seven conspired against him, they had been making their preparations for a siege during that whole period of confusion, and somehow they managed to do this without being detected. When they openly revolted, they did as follows: setting aside their mothers, each man chose one woman from his own household, whichever one he wished, and then gathered all the rest together and strangled them. Each man kept back one woman to serve as a bread-maker; they strangled the others so that they would not consume their grain supplies.

151. When Darius learned of this, he assembled all his forces and marched against them. Advancing upon Babylon, he laid siege to it, but the Babylonians cared nothing for the siege. Climbing up onto the battlements of their walls, they would dance and mock Darius and his army, and one of them called out these words: "Why do you sit there, Persians, instead of going away? You will capture us only when mules give birth." The man who said this had no expectation whatsoever that a mule could ever give birth.

150. When the fleet had departed for Samos, the Babylonians revolted — and they had made very thorough preparations for this. During the reign of the false Smerdis the Magian, and during the uprising of the seven conspirators, they had used the time and the general disorder to ready themselves for a siege. Somehow — and I cannot explain how — this went undetected. At last they rose openly, and their first act was to send away all the women. Each man kept one woman from his own household to serve as a bread-maker; all the rest were gathered together and strangled, so that they would not consume the food supplies.

151. When Darius heard of this, he assembled his full forces and marched against Babylon, laying siege to the city. But the townspeople were entirely unconcerned by what he was doing. They climbed up onto the battlements of the walls and mocked Darius and his army with gestures and words. One of them called out: "Why are you sitting there, Persians, instead of going home? You will take our city when mules give birth to foals." The Babylonian said this believing that a mule could never bear offspring.

152. A year and seven months passed, and Darius and his entire army grew increasingly frustrated at their failure to take Babylon. Yet Darius had tried every stratagem and device against it.

Darius had used every trick against them, but even so he could not take them; he tried among other stratagems the very one by which Cyrus had taken them before, but the Babylonians were keeping such an excellent watch that he could not capture them.

153. Then in the twentieth month a portent occurred for Zopyrus, the son of Megabyzus — that Megabyzus who was one of the seven men who had brought down the Magus. The portent was this: one of the mules that carried his grain gave birth. When this was reported to him, and Zopyrus himself saw the newborn in disbelief, he forbade those who had seen it to tell anyone, and he began to deliberate. And considering the words of the Babylonian who had said from the beginning that the city would be taken when mules gave birth, Zopyrus concluded from this omen that Babylon could now be captured; for he believed it was by divine will both that the man had spoken those words and that his own mule had given birth.

154. Since it seemed to him that it was now fated for Babylon to be taken, he went to Darius and asked whether he considered the capture of Babylon a matter of the greatest importance. Learning that Darius valued it very highly, he devised a new plan — how he himself might be the one to take it and make the achievement his own credit; for among the Persians, great deeds are rewarded with great advancement in honor. He could think of no other way to bring the city under his power except by mutilating himself and going over to the enemy as a deserter. Taking this as a small price to pay, he inflicted on himself a wound past healing: he cut off his own nose and ears, shaved his hair in a degrading manner, and after flogging himself, came before Darius.

He tried every device against the city. He attempted the stratagem by which Cyrus had taken it, and every other stratagem and trick, but without success; for the Babylonians kept an extraordinarily vigilant watch, and he could not take the city.

153. But in the twentieth month of the siege, something remarkable happened to Zopyrus, the son of that Megabyzus who was one of the seven men who had overthrown the Magian: one of his mules that carried his food gave birth. Zopyrus refused to believe the news, but when he went and saw the newborn foal with his own eyes, he ordered those who had witnessed it to tell no one. He then reflected on the Babylonians' saying at the start of the siege — that the city would be taken when mules gave birth — and keeping that prophecy in mind, he concluded that Babylon could indeed be taken; for he believed that the hand of heaven lay both in the man's old saying and in the birth from his own mule.

154. Convinced then that Babylon was destined to fall, he went to Darius and asked whether he placed great value on the capture of the city. When he was assured that he did, Zopyrus began to think of a plan by which the city's fall would be achieved by himself alone; for distinguished service is greatly honored among the Persians and richly rewarded with advancement. He could think of no way to gain mastery over the city except to mutilate himself and then defect to the Babylonians. Counting it a small matter to disfigure himself beyond recovery, he cut off his nose and ears, shaved his head as a further mark of disgrace, and flogged himself, then appeared before Darius in this condition.

155. Darius was greatly distressed to see his most esteemed man mutilated; he leapt from his throne and cried out, asking who had done this to him and what the man had done to deserve it. Zopyrus said, "There is no one who has the power to reduce me to this state except you yourself; no one else, O King, has done this to me — I did it to myself, considering it a terrible thing that the Assyrians should mock the Persians." Darius replied, "You most reckless of men — you have given the fairest name to the most shameful act, claiming that you mutilated yourself beyond all cure for the sake of the besieged. How will the enemy be brought to submission any sooner now that you are disfigured? Were you not out of your senses to destroy yourself in this way?" He answered, "If I had told you what I was going to do, you would not have allowed it; so I acted on my own initiative. Now, if you play your part, we shall take Babylon. I will go as a deserter to the walls just as I am, and tell them that I suffered these injuries at your hands. I believe that, once I have persuaded them this is true, I shall be given command of their forces. You, on your part, from the day I enter the city, station one thousand men from your army — men whose loss will not matter — on the tenth day at the gates called the Gates of Semiramis; then seven days after that, station another two thousand at the gates called the Gates of the Ninians; then let twenty days pass, and after that bring and station four thousand more at the gates called the Gates of the Chaldaeans. And let neither the first nor the later groups carry any of the weapons of defense, nor

these men, except for their daggers — those they were to be allowed to keep. Those stationed at the towers saw him and ran down, and opening one of the gates a little, they asked him who he was and what he wanted. Standing before them, he lamented, saying that he had suffered at the hands of Darius what he had in fact done to himself, and that he had suffered these things because he had advised Darius to withdraw the army, since no means of taking the city was in sight. "And now," he said, "I have come to you, O Babylonians, bringing you the greatest good, and to Darius and his army and the Persians the greatest harm; for he shall not go unpunished for mutilating me like this — and I know all the secret paths of his plans."
