Book IV

1. After the capture of Babylon, Darius himself led a campaign against the Scythians. For Asia was flourishing in men and great revenues were coming in, and Darius desired to punish the Scythians, because they had been the first aggressors, invading Media and defeating in battle those who opposed them, and so had begun the injustice. For, as I have said before, the Scythians had ruled the upper regions of Asia for twenty-eight years, having invaded it in pursuit of the Cimmerians and put an end to the rule of the Medes, who had held power over Asia before the Scythians arrived. But when the Scythians returned home after an absence of twenty-eight years, a trouble no less than that of the Median war awaited them; for they found a considerable army ready to oppose them. For the Scythian women, since their husbands had been away for so long, had been consorting with their slaves.

2. The Scythians blind all their slaves, for the sake of the milk they drink, doing it in the following way.

BOOK IV

1. After the capture of Babylon, Darius himself led a campaign against the Scythians. He saw that Asia was rich in manpower and that it yielded him great revenue, and so he wished to punish the Scythians for the unprovoked wrong they had done him when they invaded Asia and defeated those who came out to meet them. The Scythians, as I have previously shown, ruled the upper country of Asia for twenty-eight years; they had entered Asia in pursuit of the Cimmerians and had destroyed the power of the Medes, who had been the rulers of Asia before the Scythians arrived. But when the Scythians had been away from their homeland for twenty-eight years and finally returned, they found awaiting them a struggle just as difficult as the war they had fought against the Medes. They found themselves faced with a large opposing force; for their wives, their husbands having been gone so long, had been living with their slaves.
2. Now the Scythians blind all their slaves, on account of the milk they drink; and this is

When they have obtained bone pipes most resembling flutes, they insert these into the genitals of their mares and blow into them with their mouths, while others milk the mares as they blow. They say they do this for the following reason: that the veins of the mare are filled by the blowing and the udder is let down. When they have milked the mare, they pour the milk into hollow wooden vessels, and stationing the blind men around the vessels they shake the milk; whatever rises to the top they skim off, considering it to be the more valuable part, while what settles to the bottom they regard as inferior to the other. It is for this reason that the Scythians blind every prisoner they take; for they are not tillers of the soil but nomads.

3. From these slaves and the women a young generation grew up; and when these youths learned of their own origin, they opposed the Scythians as they returned from the land of the Medes. First they cut off the territory by digging a wide trench stretching from the Tauric mountains to the Maeotian lake, at its widest point; and then, stationing themselves against the Scythians as they tried to force their way in, they fought them. There were many battles, and when the Scythians could gain no advantage in the fighting, one of them spoke as follows: "What are we doing, men of Scythia? We are fighting our own slaves; we are being killed and becoming fewer, and by killing them we shall have fewer to rule over in the future. Now therefore

it seems to me that we should put aside our spears and bows, and let each man ride up to them carrying his horse's whip. For as long as they saw us armed, they considered us their equals and of equal birth; but when they see us with whips instead of weapons, they will understand that they are our slaves and, recognizing this, will not stand their ground."

4. The Scythians, having heard this, carried it out. The slaves, struck with amazement, forgot the battle and fled. Thus the Scythians ruled over Asia and, having been driven out by the Medes, returned to their own land in this manner. It was for these reasons that Darius, wishing to exact vengeance upon them, gathered an army against them.

5. The Scythians say that their nation is the youngest of all peoples, and that it came into being as follows. The first man to be born in this land, which was then a wilderness, was named Targitaus. The parents of this Targitaus they say — though I find it incredible — were Zeus and a daughter of the river Borysthenes. Of such lineage, they say, was Targitaus, and he had three sons: Lipoxais, Arpoxais, and the youngest, Colaxais. During their reign, there fell from the sky into Scythia golden objects: a plow, a yoke, a battle-axe, and a drinking cup. The eldest of the brothers, seeing these first, approached wishing to take them, but as he drew near the gold burst into flames. When he withdrew, the second brother approached, and again the same thing happened. The gold, burning, repelled both of them, but when the third, the youngest,

6. From Lipoxais, they say, are descended those of the Scythians called the Auchatae; from the middle brother Arpoxais are descended those called the Catiaroi and Traspies; from the youngest of them, the king, are descended those called the Paralatae. 7. This is how the Scythians say they came to be. They say that the total number of years from their first king Targitaos to the crossing of Darius against them was no more than a thousand, exactly that many. The kings guard this sacred gold with the greatest care, and each year they approach it with great sacrifices of propitiation. Whoever falls asleep outdoors at the festival while holding the sacred gold is said by the Scythians not to live out the year; and for this reason he is given as much land as he himself can ride around on horseback in a single day. Because the territory was large, Colaxais established three kingdoms for his sons, and made one of them the greatest, in which the gold was kept. As for the regions further to the north, beyond the neighboring peoples of that land, they say it is not possible to see or travel through them any further, because feathers are shed everywhere; for the earth and the air are full of feathers, and these are what block the view.

8. This is what the Scythians say about themselves and the country to the north of them, and this is what the Greeks who live on the Black Sea say. Heracles, driving the cattle of Geryon, came to this land, which was then uninhabited and is now occupied by the Scythians. Geryon lived outside the Black Sea, dwelling on the island which the Greeks call Erytheia, near Gadeira, beyond the Pillars of Heracles, on the Ocean. As for the Ocean, they say in theory that it flows from the rising of the sun around the whole earth, but they offer no proof of this in practice. From there Heracles came to the land now called Scythia, and being overtaken by storm and cold, he drew his lion-skin around him and fell asleep, and in that time his mares, which he had been driving under his chariot and had turned loose to graze, vanished by divine chance.

9. When Heracles awoke he searched for them, and after ranging over every part of the country he came at last to the land called Hylaia. There he found in a cave a creature of double nature, half maiden and half serpent — a viper-woman, whose upper parts from the buttocks upward were those of a woman, and whose lower parts were those of a snake. He looked at her in wonder and asked whether she had seen his mares wandering anywhere. She said that she had them herself and would not give them back to him unless he lay with her. So Heracles lay with her on that condition. But she kept putting off the return of the horses, wishing to keep Heracles with her as long as possible, while he wanted to get them back and go. At last, as she gave them back, she said to him —

11. There is also another account, to which I myself most incline: that the Scythian nomads, dwelling in Asia, being hard pressed in war by the Massagetae, crossed the Araxes river and went into the land of Cimmeria (for the land which the Scythians now inhabit is said to have anciently belonged to the Cimmerians). When the Scythians invaded, the Cimmerians deliberated as a great army bore down on them, and their opinions were divided, though both were strongly held — with the opinion of the kings being the better one. The opinion of the people was that they should withdraw and not risk their lives in defence of a land not worth fighting for; but the kings' opinion was to fight to the last for their country against the invaders. Neither side would yield — neither the people to the kings nor the kings to the people. The people resolved to depart and hand over the land to the invaders without a fight; but the kings decided it was better to die and be buried in their homeland than to flee with the people, reckoning how great had been their prosperity and what evils, by contrast, were likely to befall them as exiles from their fatherland. Having reached this decision, they divided into two equal groups and fought one another. And

that the people of the Cimmerians buried all those who had been slain by one another beside the river Tyres (where their tomb is still to be seen), and having buried them, made their departure from the land; whereupon the Scythians came and took possession of the country left empty.

12. And to this day there are Cimmerian walls in Scythia, and a Cimmerian ferry, and there is a region called Cimmeria, and there is what is called the Cimmerian Bosporus. It is evident that the Cimmerians, fleeing from the Scythians into Asia, also colonized the peninsula on which the Greek city of Sinope now stands. It is also clear that the Scythians pursued them and invaded Media, missing their road; for the Cimmerians always fled along the coast of the sea, while the Scythians pursued with the Caucasus on their right until they broke into Media, turning toward the inland route. That then is another account current among both Greeks and foreigners.

16. As for the land about which this account has set out to speak, no one knows accurately what lies beyond it; for I cannot find out from anyone who claims to have seen it with their own eyes. 17. Starting from the trading-post of the Borysthenites — which lies midmost of all the seaboard of Scythia — the first people are the Callippidae, who are Greek Scythians; beyond them is another people called the Alazonians. These latter also...

The Callippidae in all other respects follow Scythian customs, but they sow and eat grain, and also onions, garlic, lentils, and millet. Above the Alazones live the Scythian farmers, who sow grain not for food but for sale. Above these live the Neuri. To the north of the Neuri the land is uninhabited by men, as far as we know.

18. These are the peoples along the Hypanis river, to the west of the Borysthenes. But crossing the Borysthenes from the sea, first one comes to the Woodland, and then above it live the farming Scythians, whom the Greeks dwelling along the Hypanis river call Borysthenites, though they call themselves Olbiopolitans. These farming Scythians occupy territory extending three days' journey to the east, reaching a river called the Panticapes, and to the north, eleven days' sail up the Borysthenes. Above them the wilderness extends for a great distance. Beyond the wilderness live the Androphagi, a people entirely distinct and in no way Scythian. Above them is true wilderness, and no people at all, as far as we know.

19. To the east of these farming Scythians, once one has crossed the Panticapes river, the territory is occupied by nomadic Scythians, who sow nothing and plow nothing. All this land is bare of trees, except for the Woodland. These nomads range over a territory extending fourteen days' journey to the east, stretching as far as the river Gerrus.

20. Beyond the Gerrus lie the lands called—

23. Up to the country of these Scythians, all the land described is a flat and deep-soiled plain, but beyond this point the ground is stony and rough. After passing through a great stretch of this rough country, one comes to a people who live at the foot of high mountains, and who are said to be all bald from birth, both men and women alike, and to have flat noses and large chins, and to speak a language of their own, dressing in the Scythian fashion and living off trees. The name of the tree from which they live is Pontic; it is about the size of a fig tree. It bears a fruit as large as a bean, with a stone in it. When this fruit is ripe, they strain it through cloth, and a thick dark liquid runs off it; the name of this liquid is aschy. They lick this up and mix it with milk to drink, and from the thick sediment of it they make cakes and eat them. They have few sheep, for the pasture there is not good. Each man lives under a tree; in winter he covers the tree with a thick white felt covering, but in summer he leaves it without the felt. No one does them any harm, for they are said to be sacred; nor do they possess any weapon of war. And it is they who settle disputes among their neighbors;

dividing it among themselves, and whoever flees to them as a refugee is wronged by no one. Their name is the Argippaeans.

24. Up to the land of these bald men, the country and the nations before them are well known; for some of the Scythians make their way to them, and it is not difficult to get information from them, or from Greeks who come from the trading post at Borysthenes and from the other trading posts on the Black Sea. The Scythians who visit them conduct their business through seven interpreters using seven languages.

25. The land up to this point is known, but no one can say with certainty what lies beyond the bald men. For high impassable mountains cut off the way, and no one crosses them. The bald men say — though I find this unbelievable — that goat-footed men live in the mountains, and beyond them other men who sleep for six months of the year. This I do not accept at all. What lies to the east of the bald men is known for certain as inhabited by the Issedones, but what lies beyond to the north is unknown, both to the bald men and to the Issedones, except for what these peoples themselves report.

26. The Issedones are said to use the following customs. When a man's father dies, all the relatives bring sheep; then they sacrifice these and cut up the meat, and they also cut up the body of the dead father of the host. Mixing all the flesh together, they lay out a feast. They take his head, strip and clean it, and gild it, then use it as a sacred image, performing great annual sacrifices before it.

224

A son does this for his father, just as the Greeks do at their birthday festivals. In other respects too these people are said to be just, and the women have equal standing with the men.

27. These people too are known to us, but beyond them to the north are the Issedones, who report that there are one-eyed men and gold-guarding griffins. The Scythians have received this account from the Issedones and passed it on to us; we and the other peoples have adopted the Scythian name for these men, Arimaspi, for in Scythian arima means one and spou means eye.

28. The entire region described above has exceedingly harsh winters. For eight months of the year the cold there is unbearable: pour water on the ground and you will not make mud, but light a fire and you will make mud. The sea freezes over, as does the whole Cimmerian Bosporus, and the Scythians who live inside the trench march their armies across the ice and drive their wagons over to the Sindi. So winter lasts eight full months, and even in the remaining four months the cold is bitter. This winter differs in character from winters in all other parts of the world, in that during the rainy season it scarcely rains at all worth mentioning, while in summer the rain never stops. Where thunder occurs elsewhere, it does not occur here, but in summer it is abundant; if thunder comes in winter it is regarded as a prodigy and marveled at. Similarly, an earthquake, whether in summer or winter, is considered a prodigy in Scythia. Horses endure this winter well, but mules and asses

HERODOTUS

...and donkeys cannot endure it at all; yet in other regions, horses standing in the frost suffer from frostbite of their limbs, while donkeys and mules endure it.

29. It seems to me that this is also why the hornless breed of cattle does not grow horns there. My opinion is supported by a line of Homer in the Odyssey, which runs as follows:

"And Libya, where lambs are born already horned,"

rightly suggesting that in hot climates horns grow quickly, while in severe cold, animals either fail to grow horns at all, or grow them only with great difficulty.

30. These things then happen because of the cold. But I am also struck with wonder — for my account has always sought to include such digressions — that in the whole district of Elis mules cannot be bred, though the region is not cold, nor is any other obvious cause apparent. The Eleans themselves say that it is due to some curse that mules cannot be bred among them; so when the time comes for their mares to conceive, they drive them out to the neighboring peoples, and there they have the donkeys cover the mares until the mares are in foal, and then they drive them back home.

31. As for the feathers with which the Scythians say the air is filled, so that neither they nor anyone else can see further into the continent or travel through it, this is my opinion on the matter: in the lands beyond this region it snows continually, less in summer than in winter, as one would expect. Anyone who has seen heavy snow falling close at hand

[text continues]

and asses cannot bear it at all; yet in other lands, while asses and mules can endure frost, horses that stand in it end up frostbitten.
29. And it is my belief that this is the very reason why the hornless breed of oxen grows no horns in Scythia. There is a line of Homer in the Odyssey that supports my view; it goes like this:

"Libya, the land where lambs are born with horns already on their foreheads,"

by which it is rightly implied that in hot countries horns grow quickly, whereas in very cold countries animals grow horns slowly, or not at all.
30. In Scythia, then, this happens on account of the cold. But I find it strange — though it has always been the way of my inquiry to pursue side questions — that throughout the whole of Elis no mules can be conceived, even though the country is not cold and there is no obvious reason for it. The Eleans themselves say it is due to a curse that mules cannot be bred among them; and so whenever the season comes for the mares to conceive, they drive them into the neighboring countries and send the asses to them there, until the mares are pregnant, and then they bring them back home.
31. As for the feathers which the Scythians say fill the air so thickly that no one can see or travel through the land beyond, I have my own view on this. Northward of that country snow falls continuously, though less in summer than in winter, as one would expect. Anyone who has seen snow falling heavily close by will understand what I mean;

229

HERODOTUS

He knows what I mean; for snow resembles feathers. And because of the winter being of this kind, the northern parts of this continent are uninhabited. I believe that the Scythians and their neighbors, in likening snow to feathers, are speaking figuratively. So much has been said about the most distant regions.

32. Concerning the Hyperborean people, neither the Scythians say anything about them, nor do any others dwelling in those parts, except perhaps the Issedones. But as I think, even the Issedones say nothing about them; for if they did, the Scythians would also speak of them, just as they speak of the one-eyed men. But Hesiod has mentioned the Hyperboreans, and Homer too in the Epigoni, if indeed Homer truly composed that poem.

33. But by far the most the Delians say about them, claiming that sacred offerings wrapped in wheat straw are brought from the Hyperboreans to Scythia, and from the Scythians each neighboring people in turn receives them and carries them ever westward as far as the Adriatic, and from there they are sent southward, with the Dodoneans being the first Greeks to receive them; from them they come down to the Malian Gulf and cross over to Euboea, where city passes them to city as far as Carystus, after which Andros is left out of the route — for it is the Carystians who carry them to Tenos, and the Tenians to Delos. That is how these offerings are said to arrive there.

These are the sacred offerings said to have been sent to Delos. The Hyperboreans are said to have sent first two maidens bearing the offerings, whom the Delians call Hyperoche and Laodike. With them, for their safety, the Hyperboreans sent five of their citizens as escorts — those who are now called Perpherees and hold great honor at Delos. Since the envoys sent by the Hyperboreans did not return home, and they took it as a serious matter that if they kept sending people they would never get them back, they began carrying the offerings wrapped in wheat straw to their borders and entrusting them to their neighbors with the request that they be passed on from one people to the next. In this way, it is said, the offerings make their way to Delos. I myself know of a custom similar to this practiced with these sacred offerings: the women of Thrace and Paeonia, when they sacrifice to Queen Artemis, always hold the sacred offerings with wheat straw.

34. These are the customs I know those women to follow. For the Hyperborean maidens who died at Delos, the girls and boys of the Delians cut their hair in mourning. The girls, before marriage, cut off a lock of their hair, wind it around a spindle, and place it on the tomb — the tomb is inside the Artemision on the left as you enter, and an olive tree grows on it — and the boys of the Delians wind some green grass around their hair and likewise place it on the tomb.

35. Such is the honor these maidens receive from the inhabitants of Delos. These same people also say that Arge and Opis, who were likewise maidens from the Hyperboreans—

These came to bring to Eileithyia the tribute which they had agreed to pay in return for easing of childbirth, while Arge and Opis, they say, came together with the gods themselves and received other honors from them; for the women collect gifts in their names, singing the hymn which Olen, a Lycian man, composed for them, and from the Delians the islanders and Ionians learned to hymn Opis and Arge, naming them and collecting gifts (this Olen, who came from Lycia, also made the other ancient hymns that are sung at Delos), and when the thigh-bones are burned on the altar, the ashes are all scattered upon the tomb of Opis and Arge. 36. Let this much be said about the Hyperboreans. I do not tell the story of Abaris, who is said to have been a Hyperborean, and how he carried an arrow all around the earth, eating nothing. But if there are men who live beyond the North Wind, there are also others who live beyond the South Wind. I laugh when I see that many people have drawn maps of the world, and none of them has explained it sensibly; they draw Ocean flowing around the earth, which they make perfectly circular as if drawn with a compass, and they make Asia equal to Europe. In a few words I will show the true size of each of them and what shape each should rightly have on a map.

In length, Europe stretches along both the others, but in breadth it does not seem to me worthy of comparison with them. He, after he stopped digging the canal which runs from the Nile to the Arabian Gulf, sent Phoenician men in ships, commanding them to sail back through the Pillars of Heracles until they reached the northern sea, and so to return to Egypt. The Phoenicians therefore set out from the Red Sea and sailed

[The region of the] Medes, Saspires, and Colchians, stretching eastward toward the rising sun, is bounded on one side by the Red Sea and to the north by the Caspian Sea and the river Araxes, which flows toward the sunrise. 41. Such is Asia, and such its extent. But Libya comes next on this second promontory, for Libya follows directly after Egypt. The Egyptian portion of this promontory is narrow; for from our sea to the Red Sea the distance is one hundred thousand fathoms, that is, a thousand furlongs. But after this narrow stretch, the promontory known as Libya becomes very broad.

42. I am therefore amazed at those who have mapped out and divided the world into Libya, Asia, and Europe, for the differences between them are great. Europe stretches in length alongside both of the others combined, and appears to me to be beyond all comparison wider. As for Libya, it is clear that it is surrounded by the sea except where it borders Asia, and this was first demonstrated — as far as we know — by Necos, king of Egypt. When he had finished digging the canal that leads from the Nile to the Arabian Gulf, he sent out Phoenicians in ships, ordering them to sail back home by way of the Pillars of Heracles until they reached the northern sea and so returned to Egypt. So the Phoenicians set out from the Red Sea and

the southern sea. Whenever autumn came, they would put in to shore and sow the land wherever they happened to be along the Libyan coast, and wait for the harvest; then, having reaped the grain, they sailed on. In this way, after two years had passed, in the third year they rounded the Pillars of Heracles and arrived in Egypt. They reported — what I find incredible, though perhaps another may believe it — that as they sailed around Libya they had the sun on their right hand.

43. This is how Libya was first discovered to be a peninsula, and after that the Carthaginians are those who make this claim. For Sataspes, the son of Teaspes, a man of Achaemenid descent, failed to circumnavigate Libya, although he had been sent for that very purpose; he turned back because he feared the length of the voyage and the desolation, and did not complete the task that his mother had set him. For he had violated the virgin daughter of Zopyrus son of Megabyzus; and when he was about to be impaled for this crime by King Xerxes, his mother, who was the sister of Darius, interceded for him, saying that she would impose a greater punishment on him than Xerxes would — for she would compel him to sail around Libya until he completed the circuit and arrived back by way of the Arabian Gulf. Xerxes agreed to these terms, and Sataspes went to Egypt, where he obtained a ship and crew from the Egyptians, and sailed to the Pillars of Heracles. He passed through the Strait and rounded the cape of Libya called Soloeis, and sailed southward;

sailing the open sea for many months, and since he needed more time than he had, he turned back and sailed to Egypt. Coming from there to King Xerxes, he reported that in the farthest regions he had seen small people wearing garments of phoenix-red, who, whenever his crew brought their ship to land, would flee to the mountains and abandon their towns; his men did them no harm when they went ashore, taking only food from them. As for why he had not sailed around Libya completely, he gave this reason: the ship was no longer able to go forward but was stuck fast. Xerxes, however, did not believe he was telling the truth, and since he had not completed the task set before him, he had him impaled, exacting the ancient punishment. The eunuch of this Sataspes fled to Samos as soon as he learned that his master had died, carrying great wealth, which a man of Samos seized; though I know his name, I deliberately choose to forget it.

44. Most of Asia was explored by Darius. Wishing to know where the Indus River — which is the second of all rivers to produce crocodiles — flows out into the sea, he sent by ship men he trusted to report the truth, and among them Scylax of Caryanda. Setting out from the city of Caspatyrus and the land of Pactyice, they sailed downriver toward the east and the rising sun until they reached the sea, and then sailing westward through the sea, they arrived in the thirtieth month at the place from which the King of Egypt had sent the Phoenicians, of whom I spoke earlier, to sail around Libya. After that

having sailed around these peoples, Darius subdued the Indians and made use of this sea. Thus Asia too, except for the parts toward the rising sun, has been found to be similar in character to Libya.

45. As for Europe, it is clearly not known to anyone, neither whether it is bounded by sea on the east nor on the north; in length it is known to extend along both the other continents. Nor can I understand why, since it is one land, it bears three different names, all of them women's names, nor why the Nile river of Egypt and the Phasis river of Colchis were set as its boundaries (though some say the Maeotic river Tanais and the Cimmerian straits), nor can I learn the names of those who drew these boundaries, nor where they got these names. For Libya is said by most Greeks to be named after a native woman of that name, and Asia after the wife of Prometheus. The Lydians also lay claim to this latter name, saying that Asia was named after Asies the son of Cotys, son of Manes, and not after Prometheus's wife Asia — and from him the tribe in Sardis is also called the Asiad tribe. As for Europe, no one knows whether it is surrounded by sea, nor where it got its name, nor who gave it the name, unless we say that the land took its name from the Tyrian Europa. But she appears to have been from Asia and never to have come to the land now called Europe by the Greeks, but only as far as

from Phoenicia to Crete, and from Crete to Lycia. So much, then, on this subject; we will use the customary names for these things.

46. The Euxine Sea, against which Darius was campaigning, has, outside of the Scythian people, the most ignorant nations of all. For we cannot point to any nation within the Pontic region that has a claim to wisdom, nor do we know of any learned man who has arisen there, except among the Scythian people and Anacharsis. The Scythian people have, in the most important of human affairs, devised the cleverest invention of all those we know of — though I do not admire their other customs. This greatest invention is such that no invader who comes against them can escape, and if they do not wish to be found, it is impossible to catch them. For since they have no established cities or walls, but are all house-carriers and mounted archers, living not by agriculture but from their herds, and their dwellings are on wagons — how could these people not be invincible and impossible to engage in battle?

47. This has been made possible for them by the nature of their land and by their rivers acting as allies. For the land, being flat, is grassy and well-watered, and rivers flow through it not much fewer in number than the canals of Egypt. As for those rivers that are notable and navigable from the sea, I will name them: . . . the Ister with its five mouths, then the Tyres, the Hypanis, the Borysthenes, the Panticapes, the Hypacyris, the Gerrhus, and the Tanais. They flow as follows.

48. The Ister, being the greatest of all rivers . . .

50. From all these rivers mentioned, and from many others contributing their waters, the Ister becomes the greatest of rivers; for when comparing water with water one to one, the Nile surpasses it in volume — for into the Nile neither river nor spring contributes anything to add to its volume. But the Ister flows at the same level in both summer and winter, for the following reason, as it seems to me: in winter it is just what it is, and grows only a little above its natural level, because in that land almost no rain falls in winter and everything is covered in snow; but in summer the snow that fell in winter, being abundant, melts on all sides and flows into the Ister. This snow flowing into it swells it, along with many heavy rains that also fall — for it rains heavily in summer. And in proportion as the sun draws more water to itself in summer than in winter, so much greater are the waters that mix with the Ister in summer than in winter; but these two forces set against each other produce a balance, so that the river always appears to be the same level.

51. The first of the rivers of the Scythians is the Ister, and after it the Tyres, which flows from the north wind's direction and rises from a great lake that forms the boundary between the Scythian and Neurian lands. At its mouth there live Greeks who are called Tyritae.

52. The third river is the Hypanis, which rises in Scythia and flows from a great lake around which wild white horses graze. This lake is rightly called the Mother of the Hypanis. Rising from it, the Hypanis flows shallow and sweet for five days' journey, but from that point onward for four days' journey toward the sea it is terribly bitter; for a bitter spring flows into it, so extremely bitter that, though it is small in size, it mingles with the Hypanis — a great river — and makes it bitter within a short distance. This spring is situated on the border between the land of the Scythian farmers and the Alazones. The name of the spring and of the region from which it flows is, in the Scythian tongue, Exampaeus, which in the Greek language means Sacred Ways. The Tyres and the Hypanis draw close together near the land of the Alazones, but from that point each turns away, widening the space between them.

53. The fourth river is the Borysthenes, which is the greatest of these rivers after the Ister, and in our judgment the most productive not only among the Scythian rivers but among all rivers everywhere, except for the Nile of Egypt, with which no other river can be compared. Of the rest, the Borysthenes is the most productive: it provides the finest and most abundant pastures for cattle, and by far the best and most numerous fish; its water is most pleasant to drink; it runs clear alongside turbid rivers; the crops grown along its banks are excellent, and where the land is not sown, the grass grows deepest; at its mouth, vast quantities of salt form of their own accord; it furnishes large spine-less fish, called antacaei, for salting,

— and many other things worthy of wonder. Up to the territory of the Gerrhians, the river is known to flow from a northerly wind for a voyage of forty days; but above that, no one can say through whose lands it flows. It appears to flow through a desert into the country of the farming Scythians, for these Scythians live along it for a ten days' voyage. Of this river alone, and of the Nile, I cannot declare the sources — and I believe neither can any Greek. When the Borysthenes draws near the sea, the Hypanis joins it, emptying into the same marsh. Across the river from the sanctuary, on the Hypanis, live the Borysthenites.

55. The sixth river is the Hypacyris, which rises from a lake and flows through the midst of the nomadic Scythians, emptying near the city of Carcinitis, and leaving on its right the Hylaean region and what is called the Course of Achilles.

60. The same method of sacrifice has been established for all their sacred rites alike, and it is performed as follows: the sacrificial animal stands with its front feet bound together, and the sacrificer, standing behind the beast, pulls the end of the rope and throws the animal down; as the victim falls, he calls upon the god to whom he is sacrificing, then throws a noose around its neck, and inserting a stick, twists it and strangles the animal, without lighting a fire, without performing the preliminary rite, and without pouring a libation. Having strangled and skinned the animal, he turns to the cooking.

61. Since the land of Scythia is terribly short of wood, they have devised the following method for cooking the meat: after they have skinned the sacrificial animals, they strip the flesh from the bones, then put it — if they happen to have them — into local cauldrons, which closely resemble Lesbian mixing-bowls except that they are much larger; into these they put the meat and boil it, burning the bones of the victims underneath. If they have no cauldron available, they put all the meat into the stomachs of the animals, mix in water, and burn the bones underneath; the bones burn very well, and the stomachs easily hold the meat stripped from the bones; and so an ox cooks itself, and each of the other sacrificial animals does the same. When the meat is cooked, the sacrificer takes a first portion of the meat and the entrails and casts it before him. They sacrifice all manner of livestock, but horses most of all.

62. To the other gods they sacrifice in this manner...

...and these from their livestock. To Ares they sacrifice as follows. In each district governed by their rulers, a shrine of Ares of the following kind is established: bundles of brushwood are heaped up to a length and width of about three stades, but less in height. On top of this a flat square platform is made, and three of its sides are sheer, while on one side it may be climbed. Each year they pile on a hundred and fifty wagon-loads of brushwood, for it continually settles under the force of the winter storms. Upon this mound an ancient iron akinakes (short sword) is set up for each district, and this is the cult image of Ares. To this akinakes they bring yearly sacrifices of sheep and horses, and indeed they sacrifice to this god more than to all the other gods. Of the enemies they take prisoner, they sacrifice one man in every hundred, but not in the same manner as the sheep — rather in a different way. For after pouring wine over their heads, they cut the men's throats over a vessel, and then carry it up onto the pile of brushwood and pour the blood over the akinakes. That is what they do up above, while down below beside the shrine they do the following: they cut off the right shoulders of all the slaughtered men together with the arms and fling them into the air, and then, having finished with the other sacrificial offerings, they depart. The arm lies wherever it has fallen, and the body lies apart from it.

63. Such then are their established sacrificial rites. As for pigs, they do not consider them at all, and they will not keep them in the country under any circumstances.

64. Their customs regarding war are arranged as follows: when a man kills his first enemy...

HERODOTUS

A Scythian drinks the blood of the first man he kills. He brings the heads of all those he has slain in battle to the king; for by bringing a head he receives a share of whatever plunder is taken, but not if he brings none. He skins the head in the following manner: he cuts around the head near the ears, then grasps it and shakes out the skull; next he scrapes the flesh from the skin with the rib of an ox, and kneads it with his hands; when he has worked it soft, he keeps it as a kind of napkin, and hangs it from the bridle of the horse he rides, and takes pride in it. For whoever has the most of these skin-napkins is judged the best man. Many Scythians even make cloaks to wear from these flayed skins, sewing them together like a shepherd's coat. Many also take the right hands of their dead enemies, skin them — fingernails and all — and make covers for their quivers. Human skin, it turns out, is thick and bright, the most gleaming white of almost any skin. Many Scythians also flay whole men, stretch the skins on frames of wood, and carry them about on horseback.

65. Such are their customs in these matters. As for the heads themselves — not of all enemies, but of their bitterest foes — each man saws off everything below the eyebrows and cleans it out. If he is poor, he stretches only raw ox-hide on the outside and uses it in that form; but if he is rich, he stretches the raw hide on the outside and gilds the inside, and uses it as a drinking cup. They do this also with the heads of their own kinsmen if they have quarreled with them and one has overcome the other in the presence of the king. When guests whom he esteems come to visit him, he brings out these heads and tells the story of them...

he brings these heads and declares that his kinsmen started the war and that he himself overcame them, calling this an act of manly valor.

66. Once each year every governor of a province mixes a bowl of wine in his own district, from which those Scythians who have slain enemies are permitted to drink; those who have not achieved this do not taste of this wine, but sit apart in dishonor — and this is the greatest reproach among them. Those who have slain very many men drink from two cups at once.

67. There are many diviners among the Scythians, who practice divination with many willow rods in the following manner: they bring great bundles of rods, lay them on the ground and unfasten them, and placing each rod one by one they prophesy; and while pronouncing their oracles they gather the rods back together again and once more place them one by one. This is their ancestral form of divination. The Enarees, who are hermaphrodites, say that Aphrodite gave them the art of divination; they divine by means of linden bark: splitting the linden bark into three strips, they weave and unweave these around their fingers and give their prophecy.

68. Whenever the king of the Scythians falls ill, he sends for the three most reputable diviners, who divine in the manner described above; and they generally declare something like the following — that such-and-such a person (naming some citizen) has sworn falsely by the royal hearth. For it is the custom among the Scythians that the royal hearth

...which is considered the greatest oath when they wish to swear the most solemn one. The man accused of perjury is immediately seized and brought in; when he arrives, the seers declare that their divination shows he has perjured himself by the royal hearths, and that the king suffers because of it. The accused denies it, saying he has not committed perjury, and protests vigorously. When he denies it, the king summons twice as many seers; and if these too, consulting their divination, condemn him of perjury, his head is cut off at once, and the first seers divide his property among themselves. But if the newly arrived seers acquit him, still more seers are brought in, and yet more. If the majority acquit the man, it is decided that the first seers themselves shall be put to death.

69. And they put them to death in the following manner: they fill a wagon with brushwood and yoke oxen to it; they bind the seers' feet, tie their hands behind their backs, and gag them, then shut them in the middle of the brushwood; finally they set fire to it and stampede the oxen. Many of the oxen are burned alive together with the seers, while many escape with scorching when the wagon-pole burns through. They burn the seers in this manner for other reasons too, calling them false prophets. When the king puts men to death, he does not spare their sons either, but kills all the males; the females he does not harm.

70. The Scythians make oaths with those with whom they make them in the following way: into a large earthenware cup they pour wine and mix in the blood of those cutting the oath...

HERODOTUS

...those present, having pricked themselves with a bodkin or made a small cut in their arm with a knife, and then dipped a sword, arrows, a battle-axe, and a javelin into the blood; after doing this, they offer many prayers and then drink from the cup, both those who are swearing the oath and the most distinguished of their followers.

71. The burial-places of the kings are in the land of the Gerrhi, as far as the Borysthenes is navigable. There, when their king dies, they dig a great square pit in the earth, and when it is ready they take up the corpse — which has been treated as follows: the body is coated in wax, the belly slit open and cleaned, then filled with chopped galingale, incense, celery seed, and anise, and sewn up again — and they carry it on a wagon to another tribe. Those who receive the corpse when it is brought to them do the same as the Royal Scythians: they cut off part of their ear, shave their hair, cut around their arms, gash their forehead and nose, and drive arrows through their left hand. From there they convey the king's corpse on the wagon to yet another of the peoples they rule over, and those they visited before accompany them. When they have made the circuit of all the peoples, carrying the corpse, they are finally among the Gerrhi, who live at the farthest end of the territories they rule over, and there they hold the burial. Then, after placing the corpse in the grave upon a bed of rushes, they plant spears on either side of the body, lay wooden beams over it, and then cover it with wicker matting...

73. That is how they bury their kings. As for the other Scythians, when they die, their nearest kinsmen carry them about on wagons to visit their friends. 76. The Scythians too are strongly averse to adopting foreign customs, particularly Greek ones, as was demonstrated first by Anacharsis and later again by Skyles. Anacharsis, having traveled through many lands and displayed great wisdom in the course of his travels, was sailing back through the Hellespont toward Scythia when he put in at Cyzicus. He found the Cyzicenes celebrating a festival to the Mother of the Gods with great magnificence, and Anacharsis vowed to the Mother that if he returned home safe and sound, he would sacrifice to her just as he had seen the Cyzicenes doing and would establish a night-long ceremony in her honor. When he arrived in Scythia, he withdrew into the region called Hylaea — which lies along the so-called Course of Achilles and is entirely covered with trees of all kinds — and there, going into this place, Anacharsis performed the full rite of the goddess, holding a timbrel and having tied cult images to himself. Their women, however, grind cypress, cedar, and frankincense wood on a rough stone, adding water to it, and with the thick paste they produce they anoint all their bodies and faces; this not only leaves a fragrant scent on them, but when they remove the paste on the second day, their skin becomes clean and bright.

76. As for foreign customs, the Scythians — like other peoples — are remarkably reluctant to adopt those of any other country, and especially those of Greece, as was demonstrated in the cases of Anacharsis and later of Scyles. When Anacharsis, having seen much of the world in his travels and shown many proofs of his wisdom, was making his way back to the Scythian country, he sailed through the Hellespont and stopped at Cyzicus. There he found the Cyzicenes celebrating the feast of the Mother of the Gods with great ceremony, and he vowed to this same Mother that, if he returned to his own country safe and sound, he would offer sacrifice to her just as he had seen the Cyzicenes do, and would establish a nightly ritual in her honor. So when he arrived in Scythia, he hid himself in the region called Woodland — which lies beside the Race of Achilles and is thickly overgrown with all kinds of trees — and there Anacharsis performed the goddess's ritual in full, carrying a cymbal and hanging images about himself. Then some

reported him to King Saulius while he was doing these things. Saulius came in person, and when he saw Anacharsis performing these rites, he shot him with an arrow and killed him. And to this day, if anyone asks about Anacharsis, the Scythians say they do not know him, because he went to Greece and adopted foreign customs. As I heard from Tymnes, the guardian of Ariapeithes, Anacharsis was a paternal kinsman of Idanthyrsus king of the Scythians, and was the son of Gnurus son of Lycus son of Spargapeithes. Now if Anacharsis was indeed of this family, let him know he was killed by his own brother; for Idanthyrsus was the son of Saulius, and it was Saulius who killed Anacharsis.

77. Yet I have heard another account told by the Peloponnesians, that Anacharsis was sent by the Scythian king to learn from Greece, and on his return reported to the one who sent him that all Greeks were too busy for any kind of wisdom, except the Lacedaemonians, and that only these alone could hold a sensible conversation. But this story has been fabricated by the Greeks themselves; in any case the man perished as I described before.

78. So this is what happened to him because of foreign customs and contact with Greeks. Many years later, Scyles the son of Ariapeithes suffered a similar fate. Ariapeithes, king of the Scythians, had several children, among them Scyles, who was born to him by a woman from Istria and not at all a native Scythian. His mother taught him the Greek language and letters. Some time later,

Though he was king of the Scythians, Scyles had no liking at all for the Scythian way of life; he was inclined far more toward Greek customs, having been raised in that education. And so he would do the following: whenever he led the Scythian army to the city of the Borysthenites (who themselves claim to be Milesians), when Scyles arrived among them he would leave the army in the suburbs, and would himself go inside the walls, have the gates shut, put aside his Scythian clothing and take on Greek dress; wearing it, he would go about the market with no bodyguards or anyone else attending him. The gates were kept guarded so that no Scythian might see him dressed this way. He lived in every other respect according to Greek custom as well, and offered sacrifice to the gods according to Greek rites. When he had spent a month there or longer, he would leave, putting his Scythian dress back on. He did this frequently, and even built a house in Borysthenes and married a local woman to live in it.

79. When it was fated that things should go badly for him, it came about for the following reason. He conceived a desire to be initiated into the rites of Dionysus Bacchios. But just as the ceremony was about to be placed in his hands, a very great portent occurred. He had in the city of the Borysthenites the enclosure of a large and costly mansion — the very one I mentioned a little earlier — around which stood sphinxes and griffins of white stone. Into this house the god

a thunderbolt struck it and it burned entirely to the ground, but Scyles was none the less deterred from completing the initiation. The Scythians reproach the Greeks for this Bacchic worship, saying it is unreasonable to invent a god who drives men to madness. When Scyles had been initiated into the Bacchic rite, one of the Borysthenites went to the Scythians and said: "You mock us, Scythians, because we practice Bacchic rites and the god takes hold of us; but now this same divine power has taken hold of your king, and he is celebrating the Bacchic rite and is maddened by the god. If you do not believe me, follow me, and I will show you." The leading men of the Scythians followed him, and the Borysthenite led them secretly up onto a tower and seated them there. When Scyles passed by with the sacred band and they saw him in his Bacchic frenzy, the Scythians considered it a great calamity; and going out, they reported to the whole army what they had seen.

80. After this, when Scyles rode back to his own lands, the Scythians, placing at their head his brother Octamasades, who was born of a daughter of Teres, rose in revolt against Scyles. He, learning what was being done against him and the reason for it, fled to Thrace. When Octamasades heard this, he marched against Thrace. When he reached the Ister, the Thracians came to meet him, and just as they were about to join battle, Sitalces sent a message to Octamasades saying: "Why should we make trial of one another? You are my sister's son, and you hold my brother. Give him back to me, and I will give you your Scyles; and let us not risk

Sitalces took his brother and departed, while Octamasades on the spot cut off the head of Scyles. In this way the Scythians guard their own customs, and to those who adopt foreign customs they give such punishments as these.

81. As for the total number of the Scythians, I was not able to learn it precisely, but I heard differing accounts about the number; for some said they were very many and others that they were few, as Scythians go. Yet this much they showed me with my own eyes. There is a region between the river Borysthenes and the Hyphanis, whose name is Exampaeus; I mentioned this a little before these events, saying that there is in it a spring of bitter water, whose outflow makes the Hyphanis undrinkable. In this region there lies a bronze vessel, six times the size of the mixing-bowl at the mouth of the Black Sea which Pausanias son of Cleombrotus dedicated. For anyone who has not yet seen that one, I will describe it thus: the Scythian bronze vessel easily holds six hundred amphoras, and the thickness of this Scythian bronze vessel is six fingers. The locals said that it was made from arrowheads. For their king, whose name was Ariantes, wishing to know the total number of the Scythians, ordered every Scythian to bring one arrowhead each—

93. Before reaching the Ister, the first people he subdued were the Getae, who believe themselves immortal. The Thracians who hold Salmydessus and those living above the cities of Apollonia and Mesambria, called the Cyrmianaeans and Nipsaeans, surrendered themselves to Darius without a fight. 94. Their belief in their own immortality is as follows: they believe they do not die, but that the one who perishes goes to the deity Salmoxis — some of them call this same being Gebeleizis. Every five years they send one of their number, chosen by lot, as a messenger to Salmoxis, with instructions for whatever they need at the time. The manner of sending is this: some of those appointed hold three javelins, while others take the messenger to Salmoxis by his hands and feet, swing him up into the air, and hurl him onto the spear-points. If he dies, pierced through, the god is thought to be favorable to them; but if he does not die, they blame the messenger himself, calling him a wicked man, and after blaming him they send another in his place — though they give him his instructions while he is still alive. These same Thracians also shoot arrows up at thunder and lightning,

93. But before he came to the Ister, he first subdued the Getae, who claim to be immortal. 95. As I learn from the Greeks who live along the Hellespont and the Pontus, this Salmoxis was a human being who had been a slave in Samos — a slave of Pythagoras the son of Mnesarchus. After gaining his freedom he acquired great wealth, and having done so returned to his own country. Now the Thracians lived miserably and were rather simple-minded, and this Salmoxis knew the Ionian way of life and customs more refined than those of Thrace, having lived among Greeks and having known Pythagoras, who was no weak thinker among the Greeks. He therefore built a banqueting hall, where he entertained the leading men of the city, and while feasting them he taught them that neither he himself, nor his drinking companions, nor any of their descendants would ever die, but that they would go to a place where they would live forever and possess every good thing. While he was doing and saying these things, he was constructing an underground chamber. When the chamber was completely finished, he disappeared from the sight of the Thracians, descending into the underground chamber, where he lived for three years. The Thracians missed him and mourned for him as dead. Then in the fourth year he appeared again to the Thracians, and in this way they found what Salmoxis had told them credible. This is the story told of what he did.

96. As for myself, I neither entirely disbelieve nor fully believe this story about him and the underground chamber. But I think that this Salmoxis lived many years before Pythagoras. Whether

whether Salmoxis was a man or a native god of the Getae, let that be.

97. These people, then, having been subdued in this manner, followed the rest of the army. When Darius arrived with his infantry at the Ister, and all had crossed, he ordered the Ionians to break up the bridge and follow him by land, along with the troops from the ships. The Ionians were on the point of breaking up the bridge and doing as commanded, when Coes son of Erxander, general of the Mytileneans, first asked Darius whether he was willing to hear the opinion of one who wished to offer it. "O King," he said, "you are about to march into a land where you will find no tilled fields and no inhabited city. Keep this bridge where it is, and leave as its guards the men who built it. If we find the Scythians and things go as we wish, we have a way home; and if we cannot find them, at least our way home is secure. My fear has never been that we might be defeated by the Scythians in battle, but rather that we might suffer some harm wandering about unable to find them. One might say I speak this way for my own sake, wishing to stay behind; but in truth I bring forward what I believe to be the best counsel for you, O King, and I myself will follow you and would not be left behind." Darius was greatly pleased by this advice, and answered him thus: "Friend of Lesbos, when I return safely home, come to me without fail, so that I may repay your good counsel with good deeds."

98. Having said this, and having tied knots, he...

...holding the strap, he summoned the Ionian tyrants to a conference and said to them: "Men of Ionia, let my former proposal concerning the bridge be set aside. Now take this strap and do as I say: as soon as you see me marching against the Scythians, from that moment begin loosening one knot each day. If within that time I have not returned and the days counted by the knots have passed, sail away to your own lands. But until then, since this is now my decision, guard the bridge, showing all zeal in keeping it safe and secure. In doing this you will do me great service." Having said this, Darius pressed forward.

99. Thrace projects out toward the sea in front of the Scythian land. Then, where a gulf is formed in that country, Scythia begins, and the Ister flows out into it, its mouth turned toward the east wind. I will now proceed to describe the coastal measurement of Scythia proper from the Ister. From the Ister begins the ancient Scythia, lying toward the south and the south wind, extending as far as the city called Carcinitis. Beyond that, the land that runs along the same sea and is mountainous, jutting out into the Pontus, is inhabited by the Tauric people, as far as the peninsula called the Rugged Chersonese; and this peninsula extends down to the sea that faces the east wind. For two of Scythia's boundaries run down to the sea, one toward the south and one toward the east, just as with the land of Attica; and similarly...

In this region the Taurians also occupy part of Scythia, just as if, in Attica, some other people and not the Athenians were to inhabit the Sounian promontory, the one that juts out further into the sea, stretching from Thorikos to the district of Anaphlystos. I say this by way of comparing small things with great: such is the Tauric land. For those who have not sailed around that part of Attica, I will make it plain by another comparison: it is as if in Iapygia some other people and not the Iapygians were to cut off the headland beginning from the port of Brindisi as far as Tarentum and inhabit it. I cite these two examples, but there are many others that the Tauric land resembles.

100. Beyond the Tauric country the Scythians inhabit the land above the Taurians and along the coast of the eastern sea, both the western shores of the Cimmerian Bosporus and of Lake Maeotis, as far as the river Tanais, which empties into the innermost part of that lake. Now, from the Ister inland toward the interior, Scythia is bounded by the Agathyrsians first, then the Neuri, then the Androphagi, and finally the Melanchlainoi.

102. The Scythians, reasoning among themselves that they could not repel the army of Darius in a pitched battle alone, sent messengers to their neighbors. 103. Among these peoples, the Tauri follow these customs: they sacrifice to the Virgin goddess all shipwrecked men and any Greeks they capture during their sea-raids, as I will describe. 104. The Agathyrsi are the most luxurious of men and wear gold ornaments most lavishly. They make the use of women common among themselves, so that all may be brothers to one another and, being all relations, feel neither envy nor hatred toward each other. In their other customs they have come to resemble the Thracians.

105. The Neuri follow Scythian customs, but one generation before the campaign of Darius they were compelled to leave their entire country because of snakes; for their land produced many snakes, and even more fell upon them from the uninhabited regions to the north, so that, hard-pressed, they abandoned their own country and settled among the Budini. It seems likely that these people are sorcerers. For the Scythians and the Greeks living in Scythia say that once a year every one of the Neuri becomes a wolf for a few days and then returns to his original form. I am not convinced by those who say this, but they say it nonetheless, and they swear to it as well.

106. The Androphagi have the most savage customs of all men; they recognize no justice and follow no law. They are nomads, wearing clothing similar to that of the Scythians but with a language of their own, and they alone among these peoples eat human flesh.

HERODOTUS

107. The Melanchlainoi all wear black garments — which is the source of their name — and follow Scythian customs.

108. The Boudinoi are a large and numerous nation, all distinctly blue-eyed and ruddy. Among them stands a wooden city called Gelonos; each side of its wall is thirty stades long, high, and entirely of wood; their houses are wooden, and so are their sanctuaries. For there are shrines of Greek gods there, fitted out in the Greek manner with statues, altars, and wooden temples; and every two years they hold festivals in honor of Dionysus and revel in his rites. The Gelonoi are, in fact, Greeks in origin, who migrated from the trading-ports and settled among the Boudinoi; and they use partly the Scythian language and partly the Greek. The Boudinoi, however, do not use the same language as the Gelonoi, nor is their way of life the same.

109. For the Boudinoi, being indigenous, are nomads and are the only people in that region who eat lice, whereas the Gelonoi are farmers, grain-eaters, and keepers of gardens, utterly unlike the Boudinoi in appearance and complexion. Nevertheless, the Greeks call the Boudinoi too by the name Gelonoi, which is incorrect. Their whole country is thickly covered with forests of every kind; in the densest part of the forest there is a great broad lake surrounded by marsh and reeds. In this lake otters are caught, and beavers, and other square-faced creatures, whose pelts are sewn as borders onto fur cloaks, and whose testicles are useful for treating diseases of the womb.

110. Concerning the Sauromatai, the following account is given. When

They seized the first herd of horses they encountered, and mounted them, and rode about plundering the Scythians' possessions.

111. The Scythians could not understand what was happening, for they recognized neither the speech nor the dress nor the people, and were bewildered as to where they had come from. Thinking they were men of the same age, they fought against them. After the battle, the Scythians gained possession of the dead and so discovered that they were women. After deliberating, they decided that they would on no account kill them any further, but would send their youngest men to camp near them, in a number matching that of the women, with orders to do whatever the women did. If the women pursued them, they were not to fight but to flee; and when the women stopped,

again to camp nearby. This was the plan the Scythians devised, wishing to father children by them. The young men, having been sent out, did as they were instructed.

112. When the Amazons learned that the men had come with no harmful intent, they let them be; and each day the two camps drew closer together. The young men had nothing, just as the Amazons had nothing, except their weapons and their horses, and they lived the same life as the Amazons, by hunting and raiding.

113. Around midday the Amazons would do the following: they would scatter in ones and twos, going some distance apart from one another for the sake of privacy. The Scythians, observing this, did the same. One of the young men approached one of the women who was alone, and the Amazon did not push him away but allowed him to have his way with her. She could not speak to him, since they did not understand each other's language, but she indicated with her hand that he should come to the same place the next day and bring another, making clear there should be two, and that she herself would bring another. The young man, when he left, reported this to the rest; and on the following day he came to the spot himself and brought another, and he found the Amazon waiting there with a second woman. When the remaining young men heard of this, they too won over the rest of the Amazons.

114. After this they joined their camps and lived together, each man taking as his wife the woman with whom he had first been intimate. The men were not able to learn the women's language, but the women

the women took hold of the men. Once they were able to understand one another, the men spoke to the Amazons as follows: "We have parents and we have property. Let us no longer live this kind of life, but go back among our people and live with them. We will have you as our wives and no others." The women replied with these words: "We could not live with the women of your people, for our customs are not the same as theirs. We shoot the bow, we hurl the javelin, we ride horses — but we have never learned women's work. Your women do none of the things we have just described; they stay in their wagons doing women's work, and they never go out hunting or anywhere else. We could never get along with them. But if you truly wish to have us as wives and want to show yourselves honorable, go to your parents and receive your share of the inheritance, then come back and we will live on our own." The young men were persuaded and did exactly this.

115. When they had received their allotted share of the property and returned to the Amazons, the women said to them: "We are gripped by fear and dread at the thought of living in this land — both because we have deprived you of your fathers, and because we have done great harm to your country. But since you think it right to have us as your wives, do this along with us: come, let us leave this land, cross the river Tanais, and settle there."

116. The young men were persuaded to do this as well, and —

crossing the Tanais they traveled eastward three days' journey from the Tanais, and three days' journey northward from Lake Maeotis. Arriving at the region where they now dwell, they settled there. From that time on, the women of the Sauromatae have kept the ancient customs: they ride on horseback to the hunt together with their men and apart from them, they go to war, and they wear the same dress as the men.

117. The Sauromatae use the Scythian language, but they have always spoken it corruptly, since the Amazons never learned it properly. Their customs regarding marriage are these: no virgin may marry until she has killed a man in battle; and some of them grow old and die unmarried, because they are unable to fulfill the law.

"Do not in any way stand aside and watch us being destroyed, but with one purpose let us oppose the invader. If you will not do this, we, pressed hard, will either abandon our country or, remaining, make terms with him. For what will happen to us if you are unwilling to help? ...before. For the Persian comes no more against us than against you, and he will not be satisfied, once he has subdued us, to leave you alone. We will offer you a great proof of what we are saying. 119. When the Scythians made these appeals, the kings who had come from the various nations deliberated, and their opinions were divided. Gelonus and Budinus and Sauromatus were of one mind and promised to help the Scythians; but Agathyrsus and Neurus and Androphagus and the kings of the Melanchlainoi and the Taurians gave the Scythians this answer: "If you had not been the first to wrong the Persians and start the war, then what you are now asking of us would seem right to us, and we would listen and do as you say. But as it is, you invaded their land without us and held power over the Persians as long as the god granted it to you; and now that the same god rouses them, they are paying you back in kind. We, for our part, did no wrong to these men then, and we will not be the first to do them wrong now. But if he comes against our land too and begins wrongdoing against us,

"and we will not give in,¹ but will stay where we are until we see how things turn out; for we believe that the Persians have come not against us but against those who are responsible for the wrong done."

120. When the Scythians learned what answer had been brought back, they resolved to engage in no open pitched battle, since these peoples had refused to become their allies; instead, they would withdraw and as they went would fill in the wells and springs they passed, and destroy the pastureland, dividing themselves into two divisions. To the one division, over which Scopasis was king, they assigned the Sauromatae to join forces; these were to fall back in the direction of the river Tanais along the shore of Lake Maeotis if the Persian turned against them, and then, if he retreated, to pursue him. The other two royal divisions — the great one commanded by Idanthyrsus, and the third commanded by Taxacis — were to join together, and with the Gelonians and Budinians attached to them, they were likewise to keep one day's march ahead of the Persians, retreating and carrying out the plan that had been decided upon. First of all they were to lead the Persians directly toward the territories of those who had refused their alliance, so as to involve these peoples in the war too; for even if they had not willingly entered into the war against the Persians, they would be forced into it against their will. After that they were to turn back to their own territory and attack, if it seemed good to them after deliberation.

As for the wagons in which their children and women lived, they sent them all ahead together with all the livestock, except for as much as they needed to keep back for their own sustenance, ordering them always to drive northward.

122. So these were being sent on ahead. The Scythian scouts found the Persians at about three days' march from the Ister; and having found them, they encamped keeping a day's march ahead, destroying whatever grew out of the ground. 127. To this, Idanthyrsus, king of the Scythians, replied as follows: "This is how it stands with me, Persian. we would engage you in battle all the sooner. But if you absolutely must come to that point quickly, we happen to have the tombs of our fathers here among us; come, find them and try to violate them, and then you will learn whether we will fight you over the tombs or whether we will not. Before that, unless reason moves us, we will not join battle with you. Enough said about battle. As for my masters, I recognize only Zeus my ancestor and Hestia, queen of the Scythians. To you, instead of gifts of earth and water, I will send such gifts as are fitting for you to receive, and in return for your claim to be my master, I say to you: weep." This is the speech from the Scythians.

128. The herald then departed to report these things to Darius, and the kings of the Scythians, when they heard the word "slavery," were filled with rage. They sent the division that had been stationed with the Sauromatians, under the command of Scopasis, ordering them to go and treat with the Ionians — those who were guarding the bridged Ister. As for those who remained, they decided to lead the Persians astray no longer, but to fall upon them whenever they were seen foraging for food. Watching then for Darius's men as they foraged, they carried out their plan. The Scythian cavalry would always rout the Persian cavalry, and the Persian horsemen, as they fled, would fall back upon their infantry, which would then come to their aid; and then the Scythians, having driven off the cavalry, would wheel around, fearing the infantry. The Scythians made similar attacks also by night.

HERODOTUS

129. What proved to be the greatest ally of the Persians and the greatest obstacle to the Scythians in their attacks on Darius's army, I will now describe: it was the braying of the donkeys and the unfamiliar appearance of the mules. For the Scythian land produces neither donkey nor mule, as I have already made clear, and there is absolutely no donkey or mule anywhere throughout Scythia on account of the cold. So the donkeys, braying loudly, threw the Scythian cavalry into confusion. Many times, when the Scythians were riding against the Persians, their horses would hear the braying of the donkeys and be thrown into panic, turning about in amazement and standing with their ears pricked up, never having heard such a sound before nor seen such a creature.

130. This contributed somewhat to the course of the war. Whenever the Scythians saw the Persians thrown into confusion, they would do the following in order to make them linger longer in Scythia and, by lingering, suffer hardship from want of all necessities: they would leave behind some of their own flocks with their herdsmen and ride off themselves to another region. The Persians would come up, take the flocks, and having taken them, feel encouraged by what they had done.

131. This happened many times, until at last Darius found himself at a loss, and the Scythian kings, learning of this, sent a herald to Darius bearing gifts: a bird, a mouse, a frog, and five arrows. The Persians asked the bearer what was the meaning of the gifts. He said he had been instructed to do nothing other than deliver them and return with all speed, and that the Persians themselves
