129. Strange as it is to tell, what helped the Persians and foiled the Scythians in their attacks on Darius' army was the braying of the donkeys and the sight of the mules. For, as I have previously noted, Scythia has no donkeys or mules; and indeed throughout most of Scythia no donkey or mule exists, because of the cold. So the donkeys, when they became restless, startled the Scythian horses; and often, just as the Scythians were charging the Persians, the horses would hear the donkeys bray and wheel around in fright, or stop dead with their ears pricked up, never having heard such a sound or seen such an animal before.

130. This played some small role in the war. When the Scythians saw that the Persians were rattled, they devised a plan to stay longer in Scythia so that the Persians, by remaining there, might run short of everything they needed: they would leave some of their herds behind with the shepherds and move off themselves to another location, whereupon the Persians would come and seize the livestock and feel encouraged by this success.

131. After this had happened several times, Darius found himself at a loss. Seeing this, the Scythian kings sent a herald to Darius bearing gifts: a bird, a mouse, a frog, and five arrows. The Persians asked the bearer what these gifts meant, but he replied that he had been given no instructions other than to deliver the gifts and leave as quickly as possible; let

331

he told them, if they were wise, to figure out what the gifts meant.

132. When the Persians heard this, they deliberated. Darius's own opinion was that the Scythians were submitting themselves, their land, and their water to him, reasoning as follows: a mouse lives in the earth and eats the same grain as man; a frog lives in water; a bird is most like a horse; and the arrows signified the surrender of their own fighting strength. This was the interpretation Darius accepted. But Gobryas, one of the seven men who had overthrown the Magus, held an opinion that agreed with this, interpreting the gifts to mean: "Unless you become birds, O Persians, and fly up into the sky, or become mice and burrow into the earth, or become frogs and leap into the lakes, you will not return home again, but will be struck down by these arrows."

133. Such were the interpretations the Persians made of the gifts. Meanwhile, the one division of the Scythians that had previously been assigned to guard the region near Lake Maeotis, and had now been sent to negotiate with the Ionians at the Ister, came to the bridge and spoke as follows: "Men of Ionia, we bring you freedom, if only you are willing to listen. We have learned that Darius ordered you to guard the bridge for sixty days only, and that if he did not appear within that time, you were to depart to your own lands. Now, by doing as we say, you will be free from blame both in his eyes and in ours: wait out the appointed days, and after that, go home." With the Ionians promising to do this, the Scythians hurried back with all speed.

134. After the gifts arrived for Darius, the remaining Scythians drew up their infantry and cavalry as if intending to engage in battle. But while the Scythians were in formation, a hare ran out between the two armies, and every Scythian who saw it gave chase. When the Scythians broke into confusion and shouting, Darius inquired about the commotion among the enemy. Learning that they were chasing a hare, he said to those with whom he usually discussed such matters: "These men hold us in great contempt, and now it seems to me that Gobryas spoke rightly about the Scythian gifts. Since this is now my own view as well, we need good counsel as to how our retreat may be made safely." To this Gobryas replied: "O king, I already understood the difficulty of dealing with these men from what I had heard, but coming here I have learned it even better, seeing them mock us. My opinion now is that as soon as night falls, we should light the campfires as we have been accustomed to do, then deceive the weakest of our soldiers by leaving them behind, tether all the donkeys, and withdraw — before the Scythians march to the Ister to destroy the bridge, or the Ionians decide to do something that could ruin us."

135. Such was the counsel of Gobryas. Night came on, and Darius followed this plan: he left behind in the camp the weary men whose loss would matter least, and tethered all the donkeys there. He left the donkeys and the weakest of the army for the following reasons: the donkeys were left so that

HERODOTUS

they were making a clamor. The men who were left behind were kept there on account of their weakness, but ostensibly on this pretext: that Darius himself, with the pick of the army, intended to attack the Scythians, while these men were to guard the camp in the meantime. Having given these instructions to those left behind, and having lit the campfires, Darius made all haste toward the Ister. The donkeys, deserted by the crowd, brayed all the more loudly; and the Scythians, hearing the donkeys, fully expected the Persians to still be in their place.

136. But when day came, those who had been left behind realized that they had been betrayed by Darius. They stretched out their hands to the Scythians and explained their situation. As soon as the Scythians heard this, they quickly joined forces — the two divisions of Scythians, and the third, along with the Sauromatae, the Budini, and the Geloni — and pursued the Persians straight toward the Ister. Since the Persian army consisted mostly of infantry and did not know the roads (the routes not being cut straight), while the Scythian cavalry knew all the shortcuts, they missed one another, and the Scythians arrived at the bridge well ahead of the Persians. Finding that the Persians had not yet arrived, they spoke to the Ionians who were aboard their ships: "Men of Ionia, the days of your counted number have passed, and you are no longer doing right by remaining here. Since you stayed before out of fear, now break up the crossing and depart with all speed as free men, giving thanks to both the gods and the Scythians. As for the one who was formerly your master, we will deal with him."

so that he would never again lead a campaign against any people."

137. In response to this the Ionians deliberated. The opinion of Miltiades the Athenian, who was general and tyrant of the Chersonesites on the Hellespont, was to obey the Scythians and set Ionia free. But Histiaeus of Miletus held the opposite view, arguing that each of them now ruled his city thanks to Darius, and that if Darius's power were overthrown, he himself would not be able to hold rule over the Milesians, nor would any of the others be able to rule anywhere; for every city would choose to be a democracy rather than a tyranny. When Histiaeus put forward this opinion, all who had previously favored the view of Miltiades immediately turned to this one instead.

138. Those who carried weight in the vote and stood in high regard with the king were, from the Hellespontine region, the tyrants: Daphnis of Abydos, Hippoclus of Lampsacus, Herophantus of Parium, Metrodorus of Proconnesus, Aristagoras of Cyzicus, and Ariston of Byzantium. These were the ones from the Hellespont; from Ionia there were Strattis of Chios, Aeaces of Samos, Laodamas of Phocaea, and Histiaeus of Miletus, whose opinion was the one put forward in opposition to that of Miltiades. From the Aeolians the only man of note present was Aristagoras of Cyme.

139. When these men adopted the opinion of Histiaeus, they resolved to add to it the following actions and words: to dismantle the part of the bridge facing the Scythians, dismantling as far as an arrow's range could reach—

137. Thereupon the Ionians held a council. Miltiades the Athenian, general and despot of the Chersonese on the Hellespont, advised them to do as the Scythians said and set Ionia free. But Histiaeus of Miletus held the opposite view. "Now," said he, "it is through Darius that each of us is ruler of his own city. If Darius' power is overthrown, we will no longer be able to rule — not I in Miletus, nor any of you elsewhere — for all the cities will choose democracy over despotism." When Histiaeus declared this view, all of them immediately came around to it, even though they had initially sided with Miltiades.

138. Those who stood high in Darius' favor and cast their votes were: Daphnis of Abydos, Hippoclus of Lampsacus, Herophantus of Parium, Metrodorus of Proconnesus, Aristagoras of Cyzicus, and Ariston of Byzantium — all from the Hellespont and all despots of cities there — and from Ionia: Strattis of Chios, Aiaces of Samos, Laodamas of Phocaea, and Histiaeus of Miletus, who had opposed the plan of Miltiades. As for the Aeolians, their only notable man present was Aristagoras of Cymae.

139. These men then chose to follow Histiaeus' counsel, and resolved to back it up in both deed and word: they would break down as much of the bridge as extended a bowshot from the Scythian bank, so that they might...

...so that they might appear to be doing something while doing nothing, and so that the Scythians, pressing hard and wishing to cross the Ister by the bridge, might not attempt to force their way; and to tell them, as they dismantled the part of the bridge facing Scythia, that they would do everything that was pleasing to the Scythians. These arguments they added to the proposal; and then Histiaeus answered on behalf of all, saying:

"Men of Scythia, you bring good news and have come at the right moment; what you offer us is well received, and what we offer you in return shall be faithfully rendered. As you can see, we are breaking down the crossing, and we shall spare no effort in our desire to be free. While we dismantle it, now is your moment to go and search for the Persians, and when you find them, to take vengeance on them on our behalf as well as your own, as they deserve."

140. The Scythians, believing for a second time that the Ionians spoke the truth, turned back to search for the Persians, but missed their entire line of march. The Scythians themselves were responsible for this, having destroyed the pastures for horses in that region and stopped up the water sources. For if they had not done this, it would have been easy enough for them, had they wished, to find the Persians. But in the very plan they thought best devised, they were undone. The Scythians searched for their enemies by riding through those parts of their own land where there was fodder for horses and water, supposing that the Persians too were making their escape through such country; but the Persians kept to their own former track and so, with difficulty, found the crossing. Since it was by night and

HERODOTUS

arriving and finding the bridge destroyed, they fell into complete panic that the Ionians had abandoned them.

141. There was with Darius a man, an Egyptian, with the loudest voice of any human being. Darius ordered this man to take his place on the bank of the Ister and call for Histiaeus of Miletus. He did this, and Histiaeus, hearing his call at the first summons, brought up all the ships to ferry the army across and rebuilt the bridge.

142. So the Persians escaped in this way. The Scythians searched and missed the Persians a second time. In their judgment, as free men, the Ionians are the most base and cowardly of all men; but as slaves, they say, they are the most devoted to their masters and the least likely to run away. Such is the reproach that the Scythians have cast upon the Ionians.

143. Darius, marching through Thrace, came to Sestus on the Chersonese. From there he himself crossed by ship to Asia, leaving as general in Europe the Persian Megabazus, upon whom Darius once bestowed an honor by saying the following words among the Persians: when Darius was about to eat a pomegranate, and had opened the first one, his brother Artabanus asked him what he would wish to have in as great a number as the seeds in the pomegranate. Darius replied that he would rather have that many Megabazuses than have Greece as a subject. Having said this, he honored him among the Persians, and at that time he

When they reached it at night and found the bridge broken, they were gripped by terror, fearing that the Ionians had abandoned them.

141. Among Darius's followers was an Egyptian whose voice was the loudest in the world. Darius ordered this man to stand on the bank of the Ister and call out to Histiaeus of Miletus. The Egyptian did so, and Histiaeus, hearing the very first shout, obeyed: he sent all the ships to ferry the army across and rebuilt the bridge.

142. And so the Persians escaped. The Scythians searched for them but missed them again. Their verdict on the Ionians is this: if they are counted as free men, they are the most cowardly wretches alive; but if they are counted as slaves, none could be more devoted to their masters, or less inclined to run away. Such is the taunt the Scythians have leveled at the Ionians.

143. Darius marched through Thrace to Sestos on the Chersonese, then crossed with his fleet to Asia. He left as his commander in Europe a Persian named Megabazus, to whom he had once paid a remarkable compliment among the Persians, which I will now record. Darius was about to eat some pomegranates, and no sooner had he opened the first one than his brother Artabanus asked him what he would most wish to have in as great a number as the seeds in that pomegranate. Darius answered that he would rather have that many men like Megabazus than make all of Greece his subject. By saying this among the Persians, the king honored Megabazus; and

343

he left behind as general a force of eighty thousand from his own army.

144. This Megabazos, by uttering the following saying, left behind an immortal memory among the people of the Hellespont. When he was at Byzantium, he learned that the Chalcedonians had founded their settlement seventeen years before the Byzantines; and upon learning this he said that the Chalcedonians must have been blind at that time, for they would never have chosen the inferior site when a better one was available, had they not been blind. This same Megabazos, left behind as general in the territory of the Hellespontines, was now subjugating all those who did not take the side of the Medes.

145. So much for his activities. At this same time a great fleet was being assembled against Libya, for a reason which I will explain after first giving the following background. The descendants of the crew who had sailed on the Argo were driven out by the Pelasgians — those who had carried off the Athenian women from Brauron — and being expelled from Lemnos by these same men, they sailed to Lacedaemon and encamped on Mount Taygetus, where they lit a fire. The Lacedaemonians, seeing this, sent a messenger to ask who they were and where they came from. They told the messenger that they were Minyans, descendants of the heroes who had sailed on the Argo, and that those men had put in at Lemnos and fathered them. The Lacedaemonians, having heard the account of the Minyans' lineage, sent again a second time to ask what their purpose was in coming to their land and lighting a fire. They replied that they had been driven out by the Pelasgians and had come to their fathers, for it was most just

for this was how it had come about; and they asked to live among the Spartans, sharing in their honors and receiving allotments of land. The Lacedaemonians agreed to receive the Minyans on whatever terms the Minyans themselves wished. What chiefly moved them to do this was the voyage of the sons of Tyndareus on the Argo. So they received the Minyans, gave them a share of the land, and distributed them among the tribes. The Minyans straightaway married wives, and gave the women they had brought from Lemnos to other men.

146. Not much time had passed before the Minyans began to behave outrageously, demanding a share of the kingship and committing other impious acts. The Lacedaemonians therefore resolved to put them to death; they seized them and threw them into prison. Now the Lacedaemonians execute those they mean to kill at night, never by day. When they were on the point of putting the Minyans to death, the wives of the Minyans — who were citizens and daughters of the foremost Spartans — asked to be allowed to enter the prison and speak each with her own husband. The Spartans let them in, suspecting no trick from them. But when the women had entered, they did as follows: they gave all the clothing they were wearing to their husbands and took the men's clothing for themselves. The Minyans put on the women's garments and walked out disguised as women, and having escaped in this manner, they settled once more on Mount Taygetus.

146. Before long, however, the Minyae grew arrogant, demanding an equal share in the kingship and committing other unlawful acts. The Lacedaemonians therefore decided to put them to death, seized them, and threw them into prison. (When the Lacedaemonians execute anyone, they do so at night, never by day.) Now, as they were about to kill the prisoners, the wives of the Minyae — who were native to the land and daughters of leading Spartans — begged permission to enter the prison and speak privately with their husbands. These people inhabited the island then called Calliste for eight generations of men before Theras came from Lacedaemon.

148. It was to these people that Theras set out, taking a body of men from the tribes, intending to settle among them and by no means to drive them out, but regarding them as close kin. When the Minyans, having broken out of prison, took their seat on Mount Taygetus, and the Lacedaemonians were deliberating how to destroy them, Theras interceded so that no slaughter should take place, and undertook personally to lead them out of the country. Among those who accompanied him were other citizens, including Battus.

152. But these men were away for longer than the agreed time, and Corobius' supplies ran completely out.

After these events, a Samian ship whose master was Kolaios, while sailing toward Egypt, was carried off course to this island of Platea. The Samians learned the whole story from Korobios, left him provisions for a year, and then set sail from the island, eager to reach Egypt. They were carried along by an east wind, and since it did not let up, they sailed through the Pillars of Herakles and arrived at Tartessos, guided by divine providence. This trading post was untouched at that time, and so when they returned home, these men made the greatest profit from their cargo of all Greeks of whom we have certain knowledge — with the exception of Sostratos son of Laodamas of Aegina, for no one can rival him. The Samians took a tenth of their profits, six talents, and had made from it a bronze vessel in the Argolic style; around it are projecting griffin heads, and they dedicated it in the Heraion, setting beneath it three colossal bronze figures seven cubits tall, kneeling on their knees. From this deed, a great friendship was first established between the Cyrenaeans and Theraeans on the one side and the Samians on the other.

153. The Theraeans, after leaving Korobios on the island and returning to Thera, reported that an island had been settled off Libya. The Theraeans decided by lot to send one brother from each pair of brothers, drawing from all seven of their districts, and that Battos should be their leader and king. So they sent two fifty-oared ships to Platea.

154. This is what the Theraeans say; the rest of the account

The Therans and Cyrenaeans are now in agreement on the following account. The Cyrenaeans do not at all agree with the Therans regarding Battus; they tell the story this way. There is a city in Crete called Oaxos, where a king named Etearchus came to rule. He had a motherless daughter named Phronime, and he married another woman over her. This new wife, proving herself a stepmother to Phronime in deed as well as name, mistreated her and schemed every sort of evil against her, and finally accused her of lewdness and persuaded her husband to believe this. So he, won over by his wife, devised an unholy scheme against his own daughter. There happened to be in Oaxos a Theran merchant named Themison. Etearchus invited him to be his guest and bound him by oath to perform whatever service he might require. Once he had secured this oath, he brought out his own daughter and handed her over to Themison, ordering him to take her away and throw her into the sea. Themison, outraged at the deception behind the oath, dissolved the bond of guest-friendship and did the following: he took the girl and sailed away, and when he was out on the open sea, in order to discharge the oath of Etearchus, he tied her with ropes, lowered her into the sea, then pulled her back up again and sailed to Thera.

155. After this, Polymnestus, a man of repute among the Therans, took Phronime and made her his concubine. In time a son was born to him with a weak and stammering voice, to whom the name Battus was given, as both the Therans and the Cyrenaeans say — though in my own opinion it was something else. Battus changed his name...

This is where the Theraean and Cyrenaean accounts begin to agree, but not before now, for the Cyrenaeans tell a completely different story about Battus, which goes as follows. There is a town in Crete called Oaxus, over which a man named Etearchus became ruler. He had a daughter named Phronime, who had no mother, but he eventually had to take another wife. When this second wife entered his household, she decided to be a true stepmother to Phronime, mistreating her and plotting every kind of evil against her. Finally she accused the girl of sexual misconduct and convinced her husband the charge was true. So Etearchus, swayed by his wife, plotted a terrible wrong against his own daughter. There was a Theraean merchant at Oaxus named Themison. Etearchus took this man as his guest and friend, and bound him by oath to do whatever service he might ask. Once this was done, he handed over his own daughter, telling Themison to take her away and throw her into the sea. Themison was furious at being deceived in this way through the oath, and broke off his friendship with Etearchus. 157. Here they lived for two years; but as everything went wrong for them, leaving one of their number behind, the rest sailed to Delphi, and upon arriving consulted the oracle, saying that they were living in Libya, but that they were no better off for it. Then the priestess gave them this reply:

"I have seen Libya's pastures: your eyes have never beheld them. Do you know them better than I? Then wondrous indeed is your wisdom."

Hearing this, Battus and his men sailed back again; for the god would not allow them to do anything short of colonizing Libya itself. This is a place enclosed on both sides by the most beautiful groves, with a river flowing along one side of it.

after the land has been divided, I say he shall one day regret it.

179. There is also another story told. When the Argo had been built for Jason at Pelion, he took on board among other things a hecatomb, and also a bronze tripod, and sailed around the Peloponnese, intending to reach Delphi. But when he was off Cape Malea, a north wind caught him and carried him away to Libya; and before he could sight land, he found himself in the shallows of lake Tritonis. While he was at a loss how to get out, the story goes that Triton appeared to him and told Jason to give him the tripod, promising to show them the channel and send them on their way unharmed. Jason obeyed, and Triton showed them the passage through the shallows, and placed the tripod in his own temple, and prophesied over it, declaring the full meaning of the oracle to Jason and his companions: that whenever one of the descendants of those who had sailed in the Argo should carry off the tripod, it would then be inevitable that a hundred Greek cities be founded around lake Tritonis. When the local Libyans heard this, they hid the tripod.

As to what they used to adorn the maidens with before the Greeks settled among them, I cannot say; but I think they were adorned with Egyptian arms, for I hold that both the shield and the helmet came to the Greeks from Egypt. They say that Athena is the daughter of Poseidon and the Tritonian lake, and that having quarreled with her father she gave herself to Zeus, and Zeus made her his own daughter. Such is their account. They practice communal intercourse among their women, not living together as couples but mingling like cattle. When a woman's child is fully grown, the men assemble together within the third month, and the child is considered the son of whichever man the child most resembles.

181. Such are the coastal peoples among the nomadic Libyans. Beyond them, further inland, is the wild-beast region of Libya, and beyond the wild-beast region there stretches a ridge of sand running from Egyptian Thebes to the Pillars of Heracles. In

along this ridge, for a distance of about ten days' journey, there are lumps of salt in large chunks piled up in mounds, and from the top of each mound cold fresh water shoots up from the midst of the salt. Around these mounds live people who are the outermost inhabitants toward the desert and beyond the wild-beast country. The first of these, ten days' journey from Thebes, are the Ammonians, who have their sacred precinct derived from the Theban Zeus; for as I have said before, the image of Zeus at Thebes is ram-headed. They also happen to have another spring of fountain water, which is lukewarm at dawn, cooler as the market fills in the morning, and by midday it is very cold — it is then that they water their gardens. As the day declines it grows less cold, until at sunset the water becomes lukewarm; it then keeps getting warmer toward midnight, when it boils and bubbles over; past midnight it cools again until dawn. This spring is called the Spring of the Sun.

182. Beyond the Ammonians, along the sandy ridge, after another ten days' journey, there is a mound of salt like that at Ammonia, with water, and people live around it. This place is called Augila. It is to this place that the Nasamonians come to harvest the dates.

183. From Augila, another ten days' journey away, there is another mound of salt, with water and many fruit-bearing date palms, as at the other places, and people live there too.

BOOK IV. 181-183

Along this ridge, at each day's journey, there are great lumps of salt formed into hillocks, and from the top of every hillock a fountain of cold, sweet water shoots up out of the salt itself. People live around these springs — those who dwell farthest toward the desert and inland, away from the land of wild beasts. The first of these peoples encountered on the journey from Thebes, ten days' travel from that city, are the Ammonians, who practice the worship of the Zeus of Thebes; for, as I have said before, the image of Zeus at Thebes has the head of a ram. They have another spring besides, whose water is warm at dawn, grows colder toward midday, and is very cold at noon — the time when they use it to water their gardens. As the day wears on, the coldness gradually lessens, until by sunset the water is warm again. It continues to grow hotter and hotter until midnight, when it boils and bubbles; after midnight it grows steadily cooler again until dawn. This spring is known as the Spring of the Sun.

182. Ten days' journey farther from the Ammonians along the sandy ridge, there is another hillock of salt like that of the Ammonians, with springs of water and people living there. This place is called Augila, and it is here that the Nasamones regularly come to harvest palm-fruit.

183. Ten days' journey again from Augila, there is yet another hillock of salt, more springs of water, and many fruit-bearing palm trees, just as at the other places.

HERODOTUS

— whose name is the Garamantes, a very great and powerful nation, who spread soil over the salt and then sow their crops. The shortest route to the Lotus-eaters is a journey of thirty days from their territory. Among them are also found the backward-grazing oxen; and the reason they graze backward is this: their horns curve forward, and for this reason they walk backward as they graze, since they cannot go forward with their horns driving into the ground. In every other respect they differ from other cattle only in the thickness and toughness of their hide. The Garamantes hunt the cave-dwelling Ethiopians using four-horse chariots; for the cave-dwelling Ethiopians are the swiftest of foot of all men of whom we have any report. The cave-dwellers eat snakes and lizards and other such reptiles. Their language resembles no other; they make a sound like bats squeaking.

184. Ten days' journey from the Garamantes there is another hill of salt and water, and around it live people called the Atarantes, who are the only people we know of who have no individual names. As a group they are called the Atarantes, but no individual name is given to any one of them. They curse the sun when it rises to its height, and besides this heap every manner of abuse upon it, because it burns and oppresses both themselves and their land. Ten more days' journey brings one to yet another hill of salt and water, with people living around it. Next to this salt hill there is a mountain whose name is

BOOK IV. 183-184

There dwell men called the Garamantes, an exceedingly great nation, who sow their crops in earth that they have laid over salt. From there is the shortest route to the Lotus-eaters' country, a journey of thirty days. Among the Garamantes are oxen that walk backward as they graze; the reason for this is that their horns curve forward, so they walk in reverse while grazing, since they cannot move forward without driving their horns into the ground. In every other respect they are like ordinary oxen, except that their hide is thicker and different to the touch. These Garamantes ride in four-horse chariots to hunt the cave-dwelling Ethiopians, for the Ethiopian cave-dwellers are faster on foot than any other people we have heard of. They live on snakes, lizards, and similar creeping things. Their language resembles that of no other people in the world; it sounds like the squeaking of bats.

184. After another ten days' journey from the Garamantes, there is again a salt hillock and a water source, where men called the Atarantes live. These are the only people known to us who have no personal names; the whole people are called Atarantes, but no individual has a name of his own. When the sun is at its most intense, they curse and abuse it in the foulest terms, because its burning heat afflicts their people and their land. After yet another ten days' journey there is again a hillock of salt, water, and people living there. Near this salt stands a mountain called Atlas, the shape of which...

HERODOTUS

Atlas is narrow and circular on all sides, and so tall, it is said, that its peaks cannot be seen, for clouds never leave them, neither in summer nor in winter. The locals say that this mountain is the pillar of the sky. From this mountain these people take their name, for they are called Atlantes. It is said that they eat nothing that has life, and that they have no dreams.

185. Up to these Atlantes I am able to list the names of the peoples who dwell along the ridge, but beyond them I can go no further. Yet the ridge itself extends as far as the Pillars of Heracles and beyond. Along it, at intervals of ten days' journey, there are salt mines and people living there. Their houses are all built of blocks of salt, for this part of Libya has no rain — otherwise walls of salt could not stand if it rained. The salt mined there is both white and purple in appearance. Beyond the ridge toward the south and into the interior of Libya, the land is desert, waterless, without wildlife, without rain, without trees, and entirely without moisture.

186. From Egypt as far as Lake Tritonis, the Libyans are nomads, eating meat and drinking milk, and not tasting the flesh of cows, for the same reason as the Egyptians, and they keep no pigs. The women of Cyrene likewise consider it wrong to eat the flesh of cows, out of reverence for Isis in Egypt, and they also observe fasts in her honor and

BOOK IV. 184–186

...of which is slender and forms a complete circle; and it is said to be so high that its summits cannot be seen, for cloud is ever upon them winter and summer. The people of the country call it the pillar of heaven. These men have taken their name, which is Atlantes, from this mountain. It is said that they eat no living creature, and experience no dreams in their sleep.

185. I know and can name all the peoples that dwell on the ridge as far as the Atlantes, but no farther than that. This much I do know: the ridge extends as far as the Pillars of Heracles and beyond. There is a salt mine on it, a ten days' journey distant from the Atlantes, and men live there. Their houses are all built of blocks of salt; this is where the part of Libya begins where no rain falls, for walls of salt could not hold firm if there were rain. The salt dug from this mine is both white and purple. Beyond this ridge, the southern and inland parts of Libya are desert and waterless; there are no wild beasts, no rain, no forests; this region is entirely without moisture.

186. Thus from Egypt to the Tritonian lake, the Libyans are nomads who eat meat and drink milk; for the same reason that the Egyptians profess, they will not touch the flesh of cows; and they raise no swine. The women of Cyrene too consider it wrong to eat cows' flesh, out of reverence for the Isis of Egypt; indeed, they even honor her with fasts and

389

festivals. But the women of the Barcaeans taste neither pigs nor cows.

187. So much for that. To the west of Lake Tritonis the Libyans are no longer nomads, nor do they follow the same customs, nor do they treat their children in the way that the nomads are accustomed to do. For among the Libyan nomads — whether all of them I cannot say precisely — many do the following: when their children reach four years of age, they burn the veins on the tops of their heads with sheep's wool, and some of them burn the veins at the temples, doing this so that flowing phlegm from the head may not harm them for the rest of their lives. They say that this is why they are the healthiest of people. And indeed the Libyans are truly the healthiest of all the peoples we know of; whether it is because of this practice I cannot say precisely, but they are indeed the healthiest. If convulsions come upon the children when they are being cauterized, they have found a remedy: they pour goat's urine on them and save them. I am reporting what the Libyans themselves say.

188. The sacrificial rites of the nomads are as follows: they first cut off the ear of the animal as a first-offering and throw it over the house, and having done this they wring the animal's neck. They sacrifice only to the Sun and the Moon. All Libyans sacrifice to these, but those who live around Lake Tritonis sacrifice especially to Athena, and after her to Triton and Poseidon.

189. It seems that the clothing and the aegises on the statues of Athena were derived from Libyan women,

390

BOOK IV. 186–189

festivals; and the Barcaean women refuse to eat swine as well as cows.
187. Such is the situation in this region. But westward of the Tritonian lake the Libyans are not nomads; they do not follow the same customs, nor do they raise their children as the nomads do. Many Libyan nomads — though I cannot say with certainty whether this applies to all of them — have the practice of taking their children at four years old and burning the veins of their scalps, or sometimes their temples, with grease from sheep's wool, so that the children may never afterward be troubled by phlegm running down from the head. They say this makes their children very healthy. In truth, no people we know of are as healthy as the Libyans; whether this is because of this practice, I cannot say with certainty, but they are certainly a very healthy people. When the children suffer pain from the burning, the Libyans have found a remedy: they soothe the burns with goats' urine. This, at least, is what the Libyans themselves say.
188. The nomads' manner of making sacrifice is to cut a piece from the victim's ear as a first-fruit offering and throw it over the house; then they wring the victim's neck. They sacrifice to no gods except the sun and moon; that is the practice of the whole nation. However, those who live by the Tritonian lake sacrifice chiefly to Athene, and after her to Triton and Poseidon.
189. It would seem that the robe and aegis depicted on images of Athene were copied by the Greeks from

HERODOTUS

the Greeks adopted. For except that the garment of the Libyan women is of leather and the tassels on their aegis are not snakes but leather straps, in all other respects their dress is the same. Indeed the very name reveals that the costume of the Palladian statues came from Libya; for Libyan women wear over their clothes smooth goatskin cloaks with tassels, dyed with madder, and from these goatskins the Greeks derived the word "aegis." I also think it was in Libya that the ritual cry first arose during religious ceremonies, for the Libyan women make great use of it and do it beautifully. The Greeks also learned from the Libyans the practice of harnessing four horses to a chariot.

190. The nomads bury their dead just as the Greeks do, except for the Nasamonians, who bury them in a sitting position, taking care when the person is breathing their last to make them sit up so that they do not die lying on their backs. Their dwellings are made of woven asphodel stalks threaded around reeds, and are portable. Such are the customs these people follow.

191. To the west of the river Triton, beyond the Auseans, the Libyans are already farmers and householders; these people are called the Maxyes. They grow their hair on the right side of their heads and shave the left, and they stain their bodies with red ochre. They claim to be descended from the men of Troy. And the

Indeed, the very name reveals that the garment worn by statues of Pallas came from Libya; for Libyan women wear hairless, tasselled goatskins over their dress, dyed with madder, and the Greeks adapted the name of these into their word "aegis." Furthermore, in my view the ceremonial chant first arose in Libya: for the women of that country sing very tunefully. And it is from the Libyans that the Greeks learned to drive four-horse chariots.

190. The dead are buried by the nomads in the Greek manner, except for the Nasamones. These bury their dead in a seated position, taking care to make the dying man sit upright when he breathes his last, so that he does not die lying flat. Their dwellings are built of asphodel stalks woven around reeds; they can be moved from place to place. Such are the Libyan customs.

191. Westward of the river Triton and neighboring the Ausees begins the territory of Libyans who farm the land and live in houses; they are called the Maxyes. They wear their hair long on the right side of their heads and shave the left, and they paint their bodies with vermilion. They claim descent from the men who came from Troy. This region, and the rest of Libya toward the west, is far more full of wild beasts and much more thickly wooded than the land of the nomads. For the eastern part of Libya, which the nomads inhabit, is low-lying and sandy as far as the river Triton, but the land to the west of this, belonging to the farmers, is very mountainous, densely wooded, and teeming with wild animals. For it is there that the enormous serpents are found, and lions, and elephants, and bears, and asps, and the horned asses, and the dog-headed creatures, and the headless ones who have their eyes in their chests — or so the Libyans say — and the wild men and wild women, and a great multitude of other beasts, not to be dismissed as fictions.

192. Among the nomads none of these exist, but instead such creatures as these: white-rump antelopes, gazelles, bubalises, and asses — not the horned ones but others that go without water (for they do not drink) — and oryx, whose horns are used by craftsmen to make the curved parts of lyres (this beast is about the size of an ox), and bassarids, and hyenas, and porcupines, and wild rams, and dictyes, and jackals, and panthers, and boryes, and land crocodiles about three cubits long, most resembling lizards, and ostriches, and small one-horned serpents. These are the animals found there, as well as those found elsewhere, except for the deer and the wild boar; deer and wild boar are entirely absent from Libya. There are three kinds of mice there: some are called bipeds, others zegeiries (this name is Libyan, but in the Greek language it means

BOOK IV. 191-192

The western part of Libya is much richer in wild animals and more heavily forested than the country of the nomads. The eastern region of Libya, where the nomads live, is low-lying and sandy all the way to the river Triton; but the land to the west of this, where the farmers dwell, is extremely hilly, wooded, and full of wild beasts. In that country one finds enormous snakes, elephants, bears, asps, horned asses, dog-headed creatures, headless beings whose eyes are set in their chests (so the Libyans say), wild men and women, and many other creatures that are not mere fables.

192. In the nomads' country, however, none of these exist; yet other animals are found there: gazelles of many kinds; asses — not the horned kind, but those called "undrinking," for they truly never drink; antelopes as large as an ox, whose horns are used to form the sides of a lyre; foxes, hyenas, porcupines, wild rams, the dictys and the borys, jackals and panthers, land crocodiles three cubits long that closely resemble lizards, ostriches, and small one-horned serpents. All these animals are found there in addition to those that exist elsewhere, except for deer and wild boar — of these two species there are none whatsoever in Libya. There are in this country three kinds of mice: the two-footed kind, the "zegeries" (a Libyan word meaning "hills" in our language),

bunoí), others hedgehogs. There are also weasels found among the silphium, very similar to those of Tartessus. Such are the animals that the land of the nomadic Libyans possesses, as far as we have been able to discover by inquiry carried to its furthest extent.

193. Next to the Maxyes of Libya come the Zaueces, among whom the women drive the chariots into battle.

194. Next to these come the Gyzantes, among whom a great deal of honey is made by bees, though it is said that far more is made by craftsmen. They all paint themselves red and eat monkeys, of which there is an abundant supply in their mountains.

195. Off their coast, the Carthaginians say, there lies an island called Cyraunis, two hundred stades in length but narrow, crossable from the mainland, and full of olive trees and vines. In it there is a lake from which the local girls, using bird feathers smeared with pitch, bring up gold dust from the mud. Whether this is true I do not know, but I write what is told; though anything is possible, since I myself have seen pitch brought up from a lake and water at Zacynthus. There are several lakes there, but the largest of them measures seventy feet in every direction and is two fathoms deep. Into this they lower a pole with a myrtle branch tied to its end, and then bring up on the myrtle branch pitch, which has the smell of asphalt but is in other respects better than the pitch of Pieria. They pour it into a pit dug near the lake; and when

and the hairy, as they are called. There are also weasels found in the silphium fields, very similar to the weasels of Tartessus. Such are the many wild creatures of the nomads' country, as far as we have been able to determine through our inquiries.

193. Next to the Maxyes of Libya are the Zauekes, whose women drive their chariots to war.

194. Next to these are the Gyzantes, where a great deal of honey is produced by bees, and reportedly even more by craftsmen. It is certain that they all paint themselves with vermilion and eat apes, which are very plentiful in their mountains.

195. Off their coast, according to the Carthaginians, there lies an island called Cyraunis, two hundred furlongs long and narrow in width; there is a causeway to it from the mainland; it is full of olive trees and vines. There is said to be a lake on this island from which the local girls draw up gold-dust out of the mud using feathers smeared with pitch. I do not know if this is truly so; I write only what is said. Yet all things are possible, for I myself saw pitch drawn from the water of a pool in Zacynthus. There are many such pools there; the largest is seventy feet long and wide, and two fathoms deep. Into it they lower a pole with a myrtle branch attached to its end, and bring up pitch on the myrtle. It smells like asphalt, but is in other respects better than the pitch of Pieria. They then pour it into a pit they have dug near the pool; and when

397

they collect a large amount, they pour it from the pit into the amphorae. Whatever falls into the lake passes underground and reappears in the sea, which is about four stades distant from the lake. And so the account of what comes from the island lying off Libya is consistent with the truth.

196. The Carthaginians also tell the following story. There is a region of Libya, and people living there beyond the Pillars of Heracles. When they arrive there and unload their cargo, they set it out in a line along the shore, then board their ships and make a smoke signal. The natives, seeing the smoke, come down to the sea, and then lay down gold in exchange for the goods and withdraw some distance away from them. The Carthaginians then disembark and examine the gold, and if it seems to them a fair price for the goods, they take it and leave; but if it does not seem enough, they go back aboard their ships and wait. The natives then approach and add more gold, until the Carthaginians are satisfied. Neither party, it is said, wrongs the other: the Carthaginians do not touch the gold until it equals the value of the goods, nor do the natives touch the goods before the Carthaginians have taken the gold.

197. These are the Libyan peoples we are able to name, and most of them paid no attention whatsoever to the king of the Medes, then or now. I have this further to say about this land: four peoples inhabit it, and no more than four, as far as we know. Two of these peoples are indigenous, and two are not. The Libyans and the Ethiopians are indigenous, the former dwelling in the northern part, the latter in the

HERODOTUS

...those dwelling to the south of Libya, Phoenicians and Greeks who had settled there.

198. It seems to me that Libya has no quality worthy of comparison with Asia or Europe, except for the region of Cinyps alone; for the land takes its name from the river. This region resembles the best lands for producing the grain of Demeter and is nothing like the rest of Libya. Its soil is black and well-watered by springs, and it suffers no harm from drought nor does it take in more than enough rain — for this part of Libya receives rainfall. Its yield of grain is measured by the same standard as that of Babylonian land. The land that the Hesperitae inhabit is also good: it yields a hundredfold when it does its best, while the land around Cinyps yields three hundredfold.

199. The territory of Cyrene, which is the highest part of that Libya inhabited by the nomads, contains within itself three seasons worthy of wonder. First, the crops along the coast ripen and are ready for reaping and harvesting; when these have been gathered in, the crops in the middle region above the coastal lands — which they call the hills — are ready for harvest; and when this middle crop has been gathered, the crop in the highest part of the land ripens and comes to fullness, so that by the time the first crop has been drunk and eaten, the last is just arriving. And so the harvest season holds Cyrene for eight months. Let this suffice on these matters.

200. The Persian avengers of Pheretime, after being sent from Egypt by Aryandes, arrived at Barca and began to besiege the city...

HERODOTUS

promising to hand over those responsible for the murder of Arkesilaos. But since virtually the entire population bore responsibility, they did not accept the terms. So they then besieged Barka for nine months, digging underground tunnels toward the wall and launching fierce assaults. The tunnels were discovered by a bronzesmith, who devised the following method: he carried a bronze shield around the inside of the wall and held it against the ground of the city. Everywhere else it held against remained silent, but wherever tunneling was in progress the bronze of the shield would ring. The Barkaians would then dig counter-tunnels at those spots and kill the Persians who were mining. So this was how the tunnels were discovered, and the Barkaians repelled the assaults as well.

201. After a long time had passed with heavy losses on both sides, and no fewer among the Persians, Amasis, the commander of the infantry, devised the following plan. Learning that the Barkaians could not be taken by force but could be taken by trickery, he did as follows: by night he dug a wide trench and laid weak timbers over it, then spread soil on top of the timbers to make it level with the surrounding ground. At dawn he invited the Barkaians to a parley, and they gladly agreed, until it pleased them to come to terms. They concluded an agreement of the following kind, swearing oaths over the hidden trench: that the oath should remain in force as long as the earth remained as it was, that the Barkaians should pay tribute to the king, and that the Persians should make no new hostile move against the Barkaians. After the oath the Barkaians

402

having trusted these assurances, they themselves came out of the town and allowed any of the enemy who wished to enter the walls, opening all the gates. But the Persians broke through the hidden bridge and rushed inside the walls. They had built the bridge for this purpose, so that it would be a binding witness: by cutting it they made the oath — that it should last as long as the ground beneath remained as it then was — no longer hold in place, since the ground had been broken.

202. Pheretima, once the chief culprits among the Barcaeans were handed over to her by the Persians, impaled them around the circuit of the city wall, and cutting off the breasts of their wives, fixed these also around the wall. As for the rest of the Barcaeans, she ordered the Persians to treat them as plunder, except for those who were of the family of Battus and had no share in the murder; to these Pheretima gave control of the city.

203. The Persians then enslaved the remaining Barcaeans and began their march back. When they arrived at the city of Cyrene, the Cyrenaeans, in observance of some oracle, let them pass through the town. As the army was passing through, Badres, the commander of the naval force, urged them to seize the city, but Amasis, the commander of the infantry, would not allow it, saying they had been sent against Barca alone, the only Greek city named. When they had passed through and encamped on the hill of Zeus Lycaeus, they regretted not having taken Cyrene. They tried a second time to enter it, but the Cyrenaeans would not let them. Although no one fought them, a fear came upon the Persians —

fell, and after fleeing about sixty stades they halted. When the army had encamped there, a messenger came from Aryandes summoning them back. The Persians happened to have asked the Cyrenaeans to give them provisions for the road, and having received these they departed for Egypt. But from that point on, the Libyans set upon those who were left behind or struggling along, killing them for the sake of their clothing and equipment, until the army reached Egypt.

204. This Persian army advanced as far into Libya as Euesperides. As for those of the Barcaeans whom they had enslaved, they took them up from Egypt to the king, and Darius gave them a village in the land of Bactria to settle in. They gave this village the name Barca, and it was still inhabited in my own time, in the land of Bactria.

205. Nor did Pheretima herself end her life well. For as soon as she had exacted vengeance on the Barcaeans and returned from Libya to Egypt, she died a horrible death — for while still alive she swarmed with worms and putrefied — so true is it that exceedingly harsh acts of vengeance by human beings are regarded with jealousy by the gods. Such then was the nature and extent of the vengeance that Pheretima daughter of Battus took upon the Barcaeans.

BOOK IV. 203-205

They fled to a place sixty furlongs away and camped there. While they were there, a messenger from Aryandes came to the camp ordering them to return. The Persians asked the Cyrenaeans for provisions for their march and received them, then set out for Egypt. But along the way they fell into the hands of the Libyans, who killed the stragglers and those at the rear of the army in order to take their clothing and possessions, and so at last they reached Egypt.

204. This Persian expedition advanced no farther than Euhesperidae in Libya. As for the Barcaeans they had taken as slaves, they were transported from Egypt into exile and brought before the king. Darius gave them a town in Bactria to live in. They named this town Barce, and it remained an inhabited settlement in Bactria into my own lifetime.

205. But Pheretime also came to a bad end and did not die well. For immediately after she had taken her revenge on the Barcaeans and returned to Egypt, she died a horrible death: her body, while she still lived, broke out in festering sores and bred worms. So clear is it that the gods are angered by vengeance that is too extreme among human beings. Such was the vengeance, great and terrible as it was, that Pheretime the daughter of Battus took upon the people of Barce.

THE WORLD ACCORDING TO HERODOTUS, 440 B.C.

This is a map depicting the known world as described by the ancient Greek historian Herodotus around 440 BC. It shows three major continental regions: Europe (EUROPA) to the north, Asia (ASIA) to the east, and Libya (the ancient Greek term for Africa) to the south. The map includes the major bodies of water known to Herodotus, such as the Black Sea (Pontus Euxinus), the Sea of Azov (Palus Maetis), the Caspian Sea, the Atlantic, and the Erythraean (Red/Indian) Sea. Peoples and places range from the Celts (Keltae) and Iberians in the far west, to the Indians and Bactrians in the far east, and from the Scythians and various northern tribes in the north, to the Aethiopians and Macrobians in the far south. The map was produced by Stanford's Geographical Establishment, London.
